records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: the lighthouse attendant is a young working man (intelligent and scientifically skilled)
records.q: To see that young man, scarcely above the grade of a working man, handling his instruments and explaining them and their uses, seeming to take for granted that we could understand--which alas! we didn't, not an atom!--inspired me with a sense of humiliation and awe.
records.t:

To see that young man, scarcely above the grade of a working man, handling his instruments and explaining them and their uses, seeming to take for granted that we could understand--which alas! we didn't, not an atom!--inspired me with a sense of humiliation and awe.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: the lighthouse built by the Cornish engineer produces light (nightly, equal to about 30,000 candles)
records.q: The enormous body of light produced nightly--equal, I think he said, to 30,000 candles--and the complicated machinery for keeping the fog-horn continually at work, when even that gigantic blaze became invisible--all this amount of skill, science, labour, and money, freely expended for the saving of life, gave one a strong impression of not only British power but British beneficence.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: shipwrecks along the Cornish coast occur almost every week in winter (during wild storms or dense fogs)
records.q: Be that as it may, the fact remains, that throughout winter almost every week's chronicle at the Lizard is the same story--wild storms, or dense fogs, guns of distress heard, a hasty manning of the life-boat, dragged with difficulty down the steep cliff-road, a brief struggle with the awful sea, and then, even if a few lives are saved, with the ship herself all is over.
records.t:
shipwrecks along the Cornish coast occur almost every week in winter (during wild storms or dense fogs), 1884, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Sunday has churchgoing morning service (in Penzance)
records.q: We wondered for the last time, as we had wondered for half a century, "what the Land's End would be like," and then started, rather thoughtful than merry, to find out the truth of the case. Glad as we were to have for our expedition this quiet Sunday instead of a tumultuous week day, conscience smote us in driving through Penzance, with the church-bells ringing, and the people streaming along to morning service, all in their Sunday best.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Lizard Town has the post-office (one of the principal commercial places)
records.q: So we walked--I ought rather to say waded, for the road was literally swimming--meeting not one living creature, except a family of young ducks, who, I need scarcely say, were enjoying supreme felicity. "Yes, ladies, this is the sort of weather we have pretty well all winter. Very little frost or snow, but rain and storm, and plenty of it. Also fogs; I've heard there's nothing anywhere like the fogs at the Lizard." So said the woman at the post-office, which, except the serpentine shops, seemed to be the one emporium of commerce in the place.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall / ] DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.
records.s: The narrator describes planning a restrained Cornwall tour with two female companions, whom she calls her “chickens,” emphasizing obedience, light luggage, health, and good spirits. She explains her long-standing desire to see Cornwall, its people, and especially Land's End, inspired by childhood stories and an interest in Cornish courage and justice. The party leaves Exeter on 1 September 1881, travels through Plymouth and other Cornish districts to Falmouth, and chooses the quiet Green Bank hotel over the fashionable Falmouth Hotel. At Falmouth, they arrange lodgings and transport for the Lizard, buy provisions, and end the first day confident that their journey is proceeding well.

records.s: Cornish folk are described by reputation as honest, simple, shrewd, and kind, with a strong sense of justice, fidelity, and bravery. records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall / ] DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.
records.s: Cornwall is presented as a grand, wild, and potentially dangerous region whose people and landscapes the narrator has long wished to investigate. The party plans to study its life simply, avoid fashionable towns where possible, and travel around its coast.

records.s: The Cornish coast is characterized as the grandest, wildest, and most dangerous coast, requiring adventurous travellers to take precautions. The narrator intends to make a circuit around it with her companions.

records.s: Falmouth is reached after the party travels through Plymouth, Saltash, Liskeard, Lostwithiel, and St. Austell. The party stays at the old-fashioned Green Bank hotel rather than the fashionable Falmouth Hotel, and from Falmouth arranges lodgings and a carriage for the Lizard.

records.l: travel and rational tourism, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall / ] DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.
records.s: The narrator argues that rational travel requires observing and enjoying rather than rushing from place to place merely to claim that a country has been seen. She maintains that the traveller's mind, not only the sights themselves, creates the real interest of travel.

records.s: The Land's End circuit is the narrator's proposed route around the Cornish coast, ending at Land's End. She intends the circuit to allow her and her companions to investigate Cornwall gradually rather than hurry through it.

records.s: Obedience to the conductor is presented as the narrator's central rule for group travel. She tells her chickens that one person must decide while the others coincide, and that a competent conductor should be trusted absolutely.

records.s: Economical travel means taking little luggage, avoiding show and huge hotels, choosing quiet and humble lodgings, and spending reasonably. The narrator also insists on useful clothing, prudent footwear, shawls, waterproofs, and avoiding needless hardship.

records.s: The narrator and her two young companions travel by carriage from Falmouth to the Lizard with Charles as their driver. Charles proves dependable and kind, but becomes sorrowful when the narrator learns that his wife died after their baby died. They pass through Trelowarren and across Goonhilly Down, where they see Cornish heath and serpentine stone. At the Lizard, the young companions explore a cove while the narrator remains above because the descent is too difficult for her.

records.s: Charles drives the narrator and her two young companions from Falmouth to the Lizard. He is a dependable, courteous Cornishman and a lifelong teetotaller; he tells the narrator that his wife died after their baby died, and he helps collect heaths and point out local features.

records.s: Cornwall is described as an old country with wild landscapes, deep-cut lanes, granite quarries, ancient associations, and distinctive plants and stones. Its air is fresh and balmy, and its people include the dependable driver Charles.

records.l: Trelowarren, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SECOND Is there anything more delightful than to start on a smiling morning in a comfortable carriage, with all one's _impedimenta_ (happily not much!
records.s: Trelowarren, the seat of the old Cornish family of Vyvyan, lies along one route from Falmouth to the Lizard. The travelers pass through its woods and ferny glades, though they do not see its subterranean chambers and galleries.

records.l: Goonhilly Down, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SECOND Is there anything more delightful than to start on a smiling morning in a comfortable carriage, with all one's _impedimenta_ (happily not much!
records.s: Goonhilly Down is a broad, flat, bare, treeless district that was believed once to have been a forest and hunting ground. The travelers wander there, gather Cornish heath, and learn about its older associations with St. Rumon and the breed of ponies called Goonhillies.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SECOND Is there anything more delightful than to start on a smiling morning in a comfortable carriage, with all one's _impedimenta_ (happily not much!
records.s: The Lizard is the travelers' destination, reached after their carriage crosses Goonhilly Down. It has white-painted buildings, shops, the Lizard Lights, a sparkling sea, serpentine rocks, and a cove accessible by a difficult descent.

records.s: The serpentine district is associated with a sharp geological line of magnesian earth. The travelers notice serpentine blocks rising through the turf and used in cottage walls and fences, and they expect to find more of it near the Lizard.

records.l: the serpentine, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SECOND Is there anything more delightful than to start on a smiling morning in a comfortable carriage, with all one's _impedimenta_ (happily not much!
records.s: Serpentine is described as a reddish and greenish stone found along the coast near the Lizard. It is used for walls, fences, and polished ornaments such as candlesticks and brooches, and even forms the stile near the travelers' lodgings.

records.l: the carriage, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SECOND Is there anything more delightful than to start on a smiling morning in a comfortable carriage, with all one's _impedimenta_ (happily not much!
records.s: The comfortable carriage carries the narrator and her two young companions from Falmouth toward the Lizard. It stops while the young companions gather blackberries and later while Charles collects heaths, and it proceeds at a leisurely pace.

records.l: the Lizard journey, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SECOND Is there anything more delightful than to start on a smiling morning in a comfortable carriage, with all one's _impedimenta_ (happily not much!
records.s: The Lizard journey begins at Falmouth and takes the route through Trelowarren and Goonhilly Down rather than the regular route through Helstone. The travelers arrive later than planned but enjoy the scenery, flowers, geological features, and unhurried carriage ride.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The narrator and companions take a difficult evening boat trip from the Lizard with Charles and the boatman John Curgenven, observing the rough sea, rocks, coastline, and wildlife. They consider rowing to Kynance Cove but turn back as darkness approaches, witnessing the sunset, moonrise, and Lizard Lights. John describes Pistol Meadow, coastal shipwrecks, coast-guard work, lifeboat rescues, and local legends connected with King Arthur. After landing, Charles and John guide the narrator along narrow Cornish hedge walls, and the party safely returns home.

records.l: the practical narrator's companions, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The narrator and companions hire a boat for an evening row from the Lizard. They struggle with the landing and rough Atlantic water, decide not to continue to Kynance Cove, observe the sunset and Lizard Lights, and return safely with help from Charles and John Curgenven.

records.l: Charles, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: Charles arranges a boatman, warns that the sea and landing can be dangerous, and attends faithfully to the narrator and companions. He points out the Lizard Lights and later guides the narrator along a narrow path on top of the hedge walls.

records.l: John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: John Curgenven is the elder boatman and stroke-oar who knows the coast and handles the boat near the dangerous rocks. He is described as an exceptionally refined, kind, weather-beaten man from one of the oldest families in Cornwall, and he later helps guide the narrator home along the hedge walls.

records.l: the coastguard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The coast-guard men are described as steady, courageous, and accustomed to traveling the coast at all hours. They help with wreck rescues and use the white-washed coastal rocks as guides on dark nights.

records.l: the fishermen of the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The lifeboat volunteers are local volunteers who join rescue efforts when ships wreck. They may be needed because the lifeboat is not always sufficient, and the parson is often at the head of them.

records.l: King Arthur, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: King Arthur is imagined in connection with John Curgenven's refined and beautiful face. The narrator considers whether Arthur ever lived and recalls the belief that he sailed to Avillion to be healed and may return someday.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: Cornwall is presented as a region with a dangerous Atlantic coast, distinctive people, old legends, shipwrecks, coast-guard courage, and unusual hedge walls. Its coastal scenery and traditions strongly shape the narrator's experience.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The Lizard has a rough sea, difficult landings, steep paths, dangerous rocks, and a coast marked by shipwrecks. It is also the location of Pistol Meadow, the Lizard Lights, and the evening boat trip.

records.l: Kynance Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: Kynance Cove lies about two miles away from the party's starting point, beyond Gull Rock and Asparagus Island. The companions consider rowing there but decide they would rather see it by daylight.

records.l: the Atlantic Ocean, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The Atlantic Ocean sends large rollers and ground-swells along the Cornish coast, even when the wind is calm. Its waves make boating and landing dangerous and are associated with storms arriving from across the ocean.

records.l: the sea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The sea is broad, dark, and rough, with hills and valleys that make rowing difficult. Foaming whirlpools surround the rocks, while the sunset, moonrise, and reflected lights make the scene beautiful.

records.l: the boat belonging to John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The boat carries the narrator and companions among the rocks near the Lizard. Its boatmen steer close to dangerous whirlpools without entering them, then turn back toward land as darkness approaches.

records.l: the sunset, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The sunset occurs during the boat trip, with the sun described as dropping like a red round ball into the sea. Immediately after its last light disappears, the Lizard Lights burst out.

records.l: Pistol Meadow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: Pistol Meadow is a green area where local people do not like to walk after dark. It is associated with the graves of foreign sailors and stories that other things walk there.

records.l: the shipwreck at Pistol Meadow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: A ship went to pieces in the cove below Pistol Meadow more than a hundred years earlier. More than two hundred foreign sailors were buried under the green mounds, while only two of a crew of seven hundred survived, both having been put in irons by the captain.

records.l: the Lizard Lights, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The Lizard Lights consist of two powerful lights that become visible when the sun sets. Their beams extend far across the ocean and are said to be visible twenty or even thirty miles away, except in fog, when a fog-horn sounds.

records.l: the lifeboat, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The lifeboat is kept at the lifeboat house, whose door invites contributions and whose key is held at a nearby house and the Rectory. It is difficult to run down to the beach on a dark winter night and is not considered sufficient by itself for rescue work.

records.l: Cornish hedge walls, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: Cornish hedge walls divide land in the Lizard district instead of fences. They are six to ten feet high and about two feet wide, forcing travelers to walk along a narrow, precarious path on top of them.

records.l: shipwrecks along the Cornish coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: Shipwrecks are described as frequent and often deadly along the picturesque Cornish coast. Every half-mile may mark a place where a ship was destroyed, sometimes with the words 'all hands lost,' and John has seen a ship disappear within ten minutes of striking.

records.l: Arthurian legends, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, "Shall we get a boat?
records.s: The King Arthur legend is connected with Cornwall through beliefs about Avillion, Lyonesse, Arthur's return, and his haunting the coast in the form of a Cornish chough. The narrator also wonders whether the Arthurian type of noble knight survives in modern Cornwall.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Charles proposes an ambitious day trip for the women travelers from Lizard Town to Kennack Sands, Poltesco, and Cadgwith, arranging to return them home for dinner and take them to Mullion afterward. The women visit Kennack Sands, admire its shore and flowers, tour the serpentine works at Poltesco, and continue to Cadgwith and the Devil's Frying-pan. They learn about the dangers of bathing and the Atlantic waves, the character of the Cornish fishing communities, and the severe hardships endured on the coast during winter.

records.l: Charles, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Charles arrives early with a detailed plan for taking the women travelers to Kennack Sands, Poltesco, Cadgwith, and later Mullion. He is attentive to the women's comfort and sightseeing, while also showing concern for his horse and arranging a demanding return journey to Falmouth.

records.l: the practical narrator's companions, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The women travelers place themselves entirely in Charles's hands and set out from Lizard Town for a full day's excursion. They visit Kennack Sands, Poltesco, and Cadgwith, collect flowers, observe local life, and admire the scenery, while regretting that they did not bring bathing dresses.

records.l: the carriage, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Charles's carriage carries the women travelers through Lizard Town and across the countryside to Kennack Sands, Poltesco, and Cadgwith. It cannot use the cliff route directly from Poltesco to Cadgwith, so Charles drives one woman inland while the younger women walk with a guide.

records.l: Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Kynance is not suitable for the day's visit because the tide will not suit until Wednesday or Thursday. It is described as having especially perfect natural bathing places, including a 'kitchen' and 'drawing-room.'

records.l: Kennack Sands, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Kennack Sands has smooth yellow sands, long Atlantic waves, rock shelters, and a solitary bay. Girls bathe there in the sea, while the women travelers explore the shore, gather flowers, and observe the dangers of the water.

records.l: Cadgwith, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Cadgwith lies in a sheltered bend of the coast and is described as one of the pleasantest nooks in summer and winter. It has a small fishing station, a comfortable village inn, a mild climate, and the nearby Devil's Frying-pan.

records.l: Lizard Town, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The women travelers depart through Lizard Town at the beginning of their excursion and later return toward it from Cadgwith. They hear there that Cadgwith's parson and his wife kindly look after invalids.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The Lizard is associated with clear blue sea, bright sunshine, fresh and bracing air, and coastal villages such as Cadgwith. It is also said to have dense fogs, though Cadgwith is protected from them by its surrounding land.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Cornwall is praised for exceptionally fine English weather, blue seas, clear skies, and a mild, bracing atmosphere. Its coast is also presented as a place where pleasure involves considerable risk and where the people are notably independent and respectable.

records.l: Poltesco, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Poltesco contains the principal serpentine works and a pretty valley with a trout-stream and wooden bridge. The women travelers visit its show-room, see objects ranging from mantelpieces to brooches, and leave wishing they could carry away more of the workmanship.

records.l: the Devil's Frying-pan, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The Devil's Frying-pan near Cadgwith is a natural amphitheatre about two acres in extent, enclosed by a high semicircular cliff. The sea enters its shingly beach through a serpentine arch, and the women travelers view its waves, jagged rocks, and flying seabirds from the grassy slope.

records.l: the serpentine works at Poltesco, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The serpentine works at Poltesco employ about a dozen visible workmen and use machinery whose hum mixes with the nearby trout-stream. A workman explains the process and shows the women travelers a range of finely made serpentine goods, including vases, candlesticks, mantelpieces, tombstones, brooches, and studs.

records.l: the serpentine, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Serpentine is the material used in the principal commerce of the district. At Poltesco it is fashioned into delicate objects whose forms are sometimes Pompeian, and the coastal rocks around Cadgwith display colors ranging from red and green to grey.

records.l: bathing in Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: Bathing in Cornwall is described as delightful when it can be safely done, generally at low water on a sandy floor near a comfortable cave. The women travelers do not bathe at Kennack Sands, but girls there play in the sea.

records.l: the Atlantic waves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The Atlantic waves at Kennack Sands are long and strong, and their recoil can take a person off their feet even in calm weather. Among the rocks and eddies, they pose a serious danger to swimmers.

records.l: the Cornish fishing communities, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The Cornish fishing communities are portrayed as observant but civil, with people commonly greeting and speaking to visitors. Their working people are described as honest, independent, and respectable, while the villages themselves can be quiet and isolated.

records.l: the serpentine industry, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The serpentine industry is identified as the one commerce of the district, centered at Poltesco. Its market is limited, especially in winter, when there is said to be no market for serpentine.

records.l: the winter hardship of the Lizard community, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, ] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.
records.s: The winter hardship of the Cornish coast includes months with little work, poor fishing, and no market for serpentine. A local man says that sometimes for four months a person does not earn a halfpenny and must save during summer to avoid starvation.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: The narrator and her companions travel with Charles and his horse from the Lizard Downs through Mullion to Mullion Cove, where they explore the sea-caves before returning to the Old Inn. Mary's brother receives them at the Old Inn while Mary Mundy is away in Helstone, but Mary returns in time to provide them with a substantial tea. At Mullion Cove, the narrator sees the serpentine rocks, the sea, an artist painting in a cave, and visitors wading through the rising tide. Charles later drives the horse toward Falmouth, while the narrator and her companions spend the night at the Old Inn.

records.l: Charles, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Charles arrives punctually, reassures the travelers about his horse, and drives them from the Lizard Downs through Mullion to Mullion Cove. He guides and assists them at the cove, helps the narrator through a sea-cave, and later arranges the carriage and directions back to the farm and Old Inn. He then plans to drive the horse to Falmouth and return when the travelers need him.

records.l: Mary Mundy, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mary Mundy is away in Helstone when the travelers first reach the Old Inn, but she returns by the evening. She welcomes them warmly, provides a substantial tea, and is described as a capable, cheerful woman who puts everything and everybody to rights. She asks them to tell the Professor that she has not forgotten him.

records.l: Mary Mundy's brother, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mary's brother receives the travelers at the Old Inn while Mary is away marketing in Helstone. He is disappointed that she is absent and speaks of being unable to manage the full house and a party's requested tea without her, though he promises to provide tea for the travelers.

records.l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: The narrator travels with her companions to Mullion Cove, explores one of its caves, and admires its rocks, sands, sea, and sunset. She watches visitors wade through the rising tide, walks back with help, and later enjoys Mary Mundy's tea at the Old Inn. She also observes the farmyard, its cows, and a donkey seen in the moonlight.

records.l: the practical narrator's companions, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: The narrator's companions travel with her to Mullion Cove and safely pass through the near cave. They answer the narrator from the rocks, help her return through the cave, gather armfuls of corn-flowers, and later stay with her at the Old Inn.

records.l: the horse, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Charles's horse has rested before setting out and travels lively across the Downs to Mullion and Mullion Cove. Charles says it is accustomed to rough roads and plans to feed and groom it well before driving it toward Falmouth.

records.l: Old Inn, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: The Old Inn at Mullion is praised in a guide-book and is associated with Mary Mundy and the Professor. The travelers stay there, receive a warm welcome from Mary and her brother, and find it comfortable despite the house being full.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Cornwall is described through its rough roads, broad Cornish speech, sea-caves, serpentine rocks, distinctive grey cows, and dramatic coastal scenery. The narrator says that one can easily believe in mermaids or anything else there.

records.l: Mullion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mullion is reached from the Lizard Down and Pradenack Down. The village contains the Old Inn, and Mullion Cove lies about a mile from it.

records.l: Mullion Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mullion Cove is reached by a rough road and a steep, unpleasant descent from the surrounding area. It has a beach, grand serpentine rocks, Mullion Island offshore, and sea-caves that the travelers visit before returning to the Old Inn.

records.l: the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mullion Cove has two sea-caves: one on the beach and another around the point that is accessible only at low water. The narrator passes through the near cave, a dark winding passage with light at both ends, damp seaweed, and stones, and reaches a secluded sandy nook beyond it.

records.l: the tide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: The tide is rising fast while visitors are in the farther cave. Several people have to wade ashore up to their knees, and the narrator realizes that she and her companions must hurry or wade through the water themselves.

records.l: Mullion Cove's serpentine rocks, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mullion Cove's grand serpentine rocks enclose the beach and the secluded nook beyond the cave. The rocks form walls around the nook and are also used for serpentine candlesticks at the Old Inn.

records.l: the sea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: The sea lies in front of the secluded sandy nook and rolls in over silver sand. From the cliff above, the narrator sees the coast toward Mount's Bay and the Land's End, with the setting sun touching the waves.

records.l: the tea at the Old Inn, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, We had just time to dine, repose a little, and communicate our address to our af
records.s: Mary Mundy serves the travelers a substantial tea with hot strong tea, a large home-baked loaf, rich yellow butter, cream, clotted cream, jam, and marmalade. She repeatedly urges them to have more and charges little for the meal.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The narrator and her companions spend Sunday, September 4th, exploring the cliffs, church, churchyard, and sea-pools around Lizard and Landewednack. They attend the church of Landewednack, observe its congregation and historic graves, and enjoy a sunset followed by moonlight. During the night, the weather changes abruptly: a violent Lizard storm brings torrential rain and fierce wind. The narrator concludes that the weather has broken, threatening the harvest festival and the companions' holiday in Cornwall.

records.l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The narrator spends Sunday with her companions walking around Lizard, attending church at Landewednack, watching the sunset, and observing the moonlit landscape. She witnesses the sudden change from a beautiful day to a violent night storm and fears that the holiday in Cornwall has been ruined.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: Lizard provides the setting for the narrator's stay and excursions. Its cliffs, garden, sea-pools, church connections, and lights are described, and it experiences a severe storm during the night.

records.l: Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: Kynance lies west of the narrator's position along the cliff path from Lizard. Its cove is visible in the moonlight, and the path toward it is described as sometimes smooth and green but elsewhere steep and hazardous.

records.l: Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: Landewednack is the parish containing the comparatively modern Lizard Town and is the destination of the narrator's afternoon church visit. Its name is said to mean the white-roofed church of St. Wednack in ancient Cornish.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: Cornwall is presented as King Arthur's country, with a distinctive seaboard population and a dramatic coastal landscape. The narrator compares its storms with storms experienced in the Mediterranean and Highlands.

records.l: the Lizard Lights, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The Lizard Lights gleam across the landscape and sea at night. During the storm's darkest phase, their ghostly light is the only illumination visible to the narrator.

records.l: the church of Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The church of Landewednack is a picturesque, most southerly church in England, with a Norman doorway, a hagioscope, a carefully tended churchyard, and preserved older features alongside modern additions. It is said to have hosted the last sermon in Cornish in 1678, and its choir sings notably well.

records.l: the Lizard storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The Lizard storm begins after a night of clear skies and silence, bringing an extraordinary deluge of rain and shrieking wind. The narrator compares it favorably in awfulness with Mediterranean and Highland storms and takes it as evidence that the weather has broken.

records.l: Sunday, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: Sunday is described as a peaceful day of rest and rejoicing, marked by a walk on the cliffs, attendance at church, a sunset, and moonlit scenery. Its calm beauty contrasts sharply with the storm that arrives during the night.

records.l: the sunset, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The sunset is watched by the narrator from the cliffs beyond the Land's End. After the sun disappears into the Atlantic, an unusual green gleam appears, and the narrator quietly leaves two young lovers who are absorbed in watching it.

records.l: the storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The storm changes the sea and sky into an indistinguishable blackness and extinguishes the visible moon and stars. Its rain and wind continue until dawn, leaving the narrator convinced that the pleasant weather has ended.

records.l: the holiday in Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The holiday in Cornwall has lasted only four days when the weather breaks. The narrator laments that the storm may spoil the holiday, as well as the planned harvest festival.

records.l: the sea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FOURTH Sunday, September 4th--and we had started on September 1st; was it possible we had only been travelling four days?
records.s: The sea appears calm and brilliantly blue during the day, with sea-birds above it and sea-pools explored by the narrator's companions. At sunset it receives the sun's final glow, while during the storm it merges with the sky into near-total darkness.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers spend a very wet day indoors at the Lizard, making a fire, reading, sewing, knitting, and decorating their ugly room with artwork. They debate whether King Arthur existed and whether it is better to believe in an impossible ideal man than to accept a low ideal. Charles visits after bringing a party to the Lizard in the storm, and the travelers later wade into Lizard Town to shop. As the weather clears slightly, they reflect on Cornish coast-life, the coming harvest festival at Landewednack, and the mysteries of the laws of the universe and sorrow.

records.l: the practical narrator's companions, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers wake to an exceptionally wet morning and decide to remain prepared and comfortable indoors. They read the Idylls of the King, do needlework and knitting, make artwork, shop in Lizard Town, and conclude that the wet day has been one of their most amusing days in Cornwall.

records.l: the fire, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers decide that they must have a fire, which requires removing their sea-holly and ferns and causes concern for their handmaiden. After initially filling the room with smoke, the fire burns properly and makes the room warm, bright, and comfortable.

records.l: the rain, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The rain falls heavily throughout most of the day, making the road to Lizard Town literally swimable and leaving the travelers wading through it. It abates somewhat in the afternoon and ceases by sunset.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers remain at the Lizard during the storm, while Charles brings a party there despite the weather. The Lizard's fogs are said to be unlike those anywhere else.

records.l: Idylls of the King, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers read the Idylls of the King all the way through, ending with The Passing of Arthur. Its account of Sir Bedivere throwing Excalibur into the mere deeply moves one of the travelers and prompts a debate about ideals and belief.

records.l: King Arthur, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers debate whether King Arthur ever existed. Some argue that, if he existed, he may have been only a rough barbarian rather than the noble figure presented by Tennyson.

records.l: the ideal man, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers discuss whether it is better to believe in an impossible ideal man than to accept and worship a worldly, mean, or base ideal. The question leads to a long and heated argument.

records.l: Charles, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: Charles appears at the travelers' door soaked but smiling, wearing no hat and carrying sympathy for his ladies. He confirms that he brought a party to the Lizard that day, and that they could not have had a dry thread left on them.

records.l: Lizard Town, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The travelers wade into Lizard Town in the afternoon to look for a shop. They find the post-office and serpentine shops, where they can buy food, drink, clothing, and various ornaments.

records.l: Cornish coast-life, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: A woman at the post-office says that Cornish coast-life in winter commonly brings rain, storms, and fogs, with little frost or snow. The storm helps the travelers understand what such life is like throughout the winter.

records.l: the storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The storm brings intense rain and shifting winds, but gradually abates. By sunset the wind has stopped and the rain has ceased, though the lanes remain flooded and the sea still looks angry.

records.l: Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: Landewednack is to hold a harvest festival the next day. The whole community and their wives are invited by shilling tickets to tea in the rectory garden and later to an evening thanksgiving service in the church.

records.l: the harvest festival, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The harvest festival is scheduled for the day after the storm and includes tea in the rectory garden followed by an evening thanksgiving service. The text questions how thankful the festival can seem to farmers after such damaging weather.

records.l: the laws of the universe, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The laws of the universe must be carried out, even when doing so causes suffering to individuals or nations. Their operation remains connected with mysteries that the text says are not explained.

records.l: the mystery of sorrow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE FIFTH "Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst," had been the motto of our journey.
records.s: The mystery of sorrow, like the greater mystery of evil, remains unexplained. The text nevertheless affirms that the world can be made marvelously beautiful despite sorrow and even after a day when it seems hardly worth living in.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: On DAY THE SIXTH, the narrator and companions enjoy a perfect autumn morning at Housel Cove, bathing in the Atlantic and idling on the shore. They spend the afternoon sketching near Kynance before attending the rectory tea, where rich and poor Cornish folk meet courteously and a village wind band plays badly. The evening church service is crowded and beautifully performed, followed by a walk through the moonlit countryside. The day ends with the wind band playing again near the hotels, while the party flees toward the familiar glow of the Lizard Lights.

records.l: DAY THE SIXTH, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: DAY THE SIXTH is described as a day of perfect autumn weather, with brilliant green pasture, gleaming yellow cornfields, and clear skies. The narrator and companions spend it bathing, sketching, attending the rectory tea and evening church service, and walking beneath the moonlight.

records.l: the practical narrator's companions, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The narrator and companions visit Housel Cove, bathe in the Atlantic, and spend the morning attempting to catch a tiny fish in a rock pool. They sketch near Kynance, attend the rectory tea and evening church service, and flee from the village wind band when its music becomes unbearable.

records.l: Housel Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: Housel Cove provides a secluded place for bathing, with soft sand and a beautiful dressing-room made of serpentine rock. The narrator and companions spend the whole morning there without band, promenade, or other organized amusement.

records.l: the Atlantic Ocean, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The Atlantic rolls to the feet of the bathers in gentle baby ripples, despite its immense distance and association with great ships going down. It tempts the narrator's two little mermaids to swim as far out as prudence permits.

records.l: the sea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The sea is watched from the shore as its waves advance toward stones, rocks, and a sandcastle. Its ninth wave is said to be the largest, and its remorseless movement is compared with the passage of Time.

records.l: the Cornish people, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: Cornish folk are presented as courteous and independent, with rich and poor meeting at the rectory tea for courtesy rather than charity. Their treatment of strangers is kind, and the narrator considers this a pleasant aspect of their human nature.

records.l: the rectory tea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The rectory tea brings together humble parishioners, elderly people, county families, and other guests. It takes place in a flower-filled garden with tea tables, lawn-tennis on sea-sand, and music from the village wind band before the congregation goes to church.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The Lizard is noted for longevity, with register books recording several deaths at over one hundred years and one rector reputed to have died at the age of 120. It contains Lizard Town, two nearby hotels, a church, and paths leading into quieter countryside.

records.l: the village wind band, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The village wind band consists of about half a dozen wind instruments that play determinedly flat, with the bass entering loudly without regard to time or tune. It plays at the rectory tea and later near the hotels, causing the narrator and companions to cover their ears and flee.

records.l: the church of Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The church is crowded for the evening service, with no seat vacant, and is decorated with exceptionally rich and tasteful flowers and fruit. Its organist, clergy, and congregation contribute to an impressive service.

records.l: the evening church service, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The evening church service includes accurate chanting, hymns, a harvest anthem, organ music, and a good sermon. An elderly clergyman reads the prayers with unusual expression, and the service ends with a brilliant organ voluntary.

records.l: the Lizard Lights, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SIXTH And a day absolutely divine!
records.s: The Lizard Lights are seen from the moonlit countryside after the evening service. Their far-gleaming appearance has become familiar to the narrator and companions but remains beautiful.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: John Curgenven guides the narrator and the girls partway across the downs toward Kynance Cove, warning them about the tide and dangerous rocks. At the Cove, the girls bathe, visit the Bellows, and climb Asparagus Island, while the narrator watches and speaks with an elderly clergyman whose daughters are nearby. The advancing tide forces the visitors to leave, and the group returns over the downs before walking to Lizard Point to watch the sunset. News of sickness and death casts a temporary sadness over the evening, though the narrator finds comfort in the moonlit landscape.

records.l: John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: John Curgenven comes to the narrator and the girls at breakfast with fish as a gift and offers to take them to Kynance Cove. He leads them across the downs, assists them over rough ground, and explains the route, the caves, the tide, and the dangers of Asparagus Island and Devil's Throat. He leaves before reaching the Cove because he has an engagement, then later sells the narrator's party serpentine through his wife.

records.l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: The narrator travels with the girls to Kynance Cove, cautiously joins them at the Bellows, and waits while they climb Asparagus Island. She speaks with an elderly clergyman about sensible bravery and foolhardy risk, helps warn her girls against Hell's Mouth, and leaves before the tide cuts off the route. She later walks to Lizard Point, hears sad news of sickness and death, and finds consolation in the moonlight.

records.l: the girls at Kennack Sands, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: The girls accompany the narrator to Kynance Cove, bathe in the waves, and enjoy themselves despite being repeatedly knocked down. They visit the Bellows and climb Asparagus Island by a difficult path, while promising not to attempt the more dangerous rocks. They return safely and later find a route along the tops of hedges to Lizard Point.

records.l: Kynance Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: Kynance Cove is reached by a path across the downs and down a steep descent. It contains richly colored rocks, caves called the Drawing-room, Dining-room, and Kitchen, Asparagus Island, the Bellows, and Gull Rock. The narrator finds it beautiful but notes that its attractions become inaccessible when the tide advances.

records.l: Drawing-room Cave, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: The Drawing-room Cave is described as the loveliest of the caves at Kynance Cove, with a floor of soft sand. The narrator and the girls retreat there after bathing, but waves soon begin to cover its floor as the tide comes in.

records.l: Asparagus Island, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: Asparagus Island has no asparagus, despite its name, and can be reached by climbing a path that the narrator considers unsafe for herself. The girls climb it successfully, and the elderly clergyman says that it is easy enough compared with the more dangerous rocks.

records.l: the Bellows, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: The Bellows is a curious feature at Kynance Cove where, under certain tidal conditions, water forces itself through a narrow fissure in the rock with a loud roar. The narrator visits it with the girls and watches for the largest spout.

records.l: Devil's Throat, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: Devil's Throat is identified by John Curgenven as a dangerous place that visitors should not attempt. An elderly clergyman warns two young people away from it while they crawl along the rock face toward a fissure and cave.

records.l: Hell's Mouth, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: Hell's Mouth is another name given for the dangerous place John Curgenven warns the party not to attempt. The narrator repeats his warning to the girls and is relieved that they do not try it.

records.l: Lizard Point, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: Lizard Point is a grand rock reached by the girls through a route mainly along the tops of hedges. The narrator and the girls walk there in the evening and watch a fine sunset.

records.l: the elderly clergyman, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: The elderly clergyman waits on the sands and calls out warnings to two young people attempting a dangerous route near Devil's Throat. He explains that his own daughters are safely climbing Asparagus Rock and says that he approves of reasonable activity but despises foolhardy bravado. He and the narrator discuss these views and become friendly companions for a time.

records.l: the tide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, DAY THE SEVENTH John Curgenven had said last night, with his air of tender patronising, half regal, half paternal, which we declared always reminded us of King Arthur--"Ladies, whenever you settle to go to Kynance, I'll take you.
records.s: The tide comes in quickly at Kynance Cove, covering the sandy floors of the caves and turning one visitor's rock into an island. The narrator's party leaves hurriedly before the route becomes impassable, while a newly arrived group is left needing to wade and possibly swim ashore.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The traveling women spend their eighth and final day at the Lizard, bathing at Housel Cove, viewing the coast, and visiting the Lizard Lights. They learn about launce-fishing, hear the lighthouse attendant's accounts of shipwrecks, and observe a perfect solar rainbow. They arrange a journey to Marazion with Charles, adding a planned boat excursion to sea-caves near Church Cove. The narrator ends the day reflecting on human mortality, death, and the possibility of an imperishable afterlife.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The traveling women spend their last day at the Lizard, where they bathe, explore the shore, visit the Lizard Lights, and prepare to leave for Marazion. They regard the place with strong affection and regret having to depart.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The women are touring Cornwall and have allowed themselves seven days at the Lizard in order to see the rest of the county. They plan to continue toward Marazion by way of Helstone.

records.l: Housel Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The women walk through the fields to Housel Cove for their bath. They find the bathing there as delightful as before.

records.l: Penolver, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: Penolver appears as a fine headland near Housel Cove. The clerical friend's daughters climb over it, and the young folks later go there for a scramble.

records.l: Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: Kynance is visible from the moonlit Lizard coast, and the women recall the clerical friend's daughters visiting it without falling into the Devil's Throat. The narrator mentions hearing the waves at Kynance during her midnight walk.

records.l: the Lizard Lights, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The women visit the Lizard Lights after watching them night after night from a distance. They see the huge white building, its enormous lamps, ladders, lighting apparatus, and fog-horn machinery, though they admit they cannot understand the mechanisms.

records.l: Marazion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: Marazion is chosen as the women's next resting-place. They are attracted by its history, its position opposite St. Michael's Mount, and a hotel landlord's promise of comfort.

records.l: the clerical friend of Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The clerical friend tells the women that his children have bathed near Kynance, walked to Cadgwith, and gone launce-fishing by moonlight. He explains how launce-fishing is performed and says his children returned home about two o'clock in the morning.

records.l: the narrator and traveling party, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The traveling women spend their last day at the Lizard bathing, observing a solar rainbow, touring the Lizard Lights, and listening to accounts of wrecks. They decide to travel to Marazion and add a boat trip to sea-caves before leaving.

records.l: chickens (the old hen's chickens), An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The young folks go walking and scrambling over Penolver while the narrator sits quietly by the sea. They return full of enthusiasm for the cliff walk and regret that the narrator could not join them.

records.l: the lighthouse attendant, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The lighthouse attendant, described as an intelligent young man scarcely above the grade of a working man, conducts the women through the Lizard Lights. He explains the instruments and recounts several wrecks he has witnessed, despite appearing sickly and having a short cough.

records.l: Charles, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: Charles arrives as agreed to take charge of the women during their journey back toward civilisation. He arranges the same carriage and horse, proposes routes through Mullion and Gunwalloe, and willingly modifies the plan to include a boat excursion to the sea-caves.

records.l: the coastguard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The coastguard men are described as picked men of the service who lead a risky life during winter rescues. Their work is said to be tolerably well paid, but no money could fully compensate them for what they endure.

records.l: the fishermen of the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The fishermen often volunteer in rescue work and receive little or nothing. They face the dangerous winter seas alongside the coastguard men.

records.l: launce-fishing, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: Launce-fishing is described as a popular Lizard pastime carried out on moonlit nights. Participants stand barefoot on wet sand, use a crooked iron spear to hook sand-eels, and may cook their catch over a fire around midnight.

records.l: the launce, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The launce is a sand-eel peculiar to the Cornish coasts. It swims during the day and burrows in sand above the waterline at night, where its silvery gleam can be seen in moonlight.

records.l: the perfect solar rainbow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The women see a rare perfect solar rainbow after bathing at Housel Cove. It forms a luminous circle around the sun, changes from yellow to faint prismatic colors, and gradually disappears.

records.l: the lighthouse built by the Cornish engineer, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The lighthouse at the Lizard is represented by the huge white building containing the enormous light and fog-horn apparatus. Its purpose is to help save ships and lives along a dangerous coast.

records.l: the lighthouse machinery, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The lighthouse machinery includes Brobdingnagian lamps, devices for producing the light, and complicated mechanisms for keeping the fog-horn working when the light becomes invisible. The light is said to equal about 30,000 candles.

records.l: shipwrecks along the Cornish coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The lighthouse attendant recounts numerous shipwrecks at the Lizard, especially near the rocks known collectively as the Stags. He says that almost every winter week brings storms or fog, distress guns, lifeboat launches, and ships breaking apart, including one that was destroyed in ten minutes.

records.l: the planned boat excursion to the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The women regret that earlier boating plans with John Curgenven have failed and that they may not see the sea-caves between the Lizard and Cadgwith. Charles proposes taking a boat from Church Cove before driving onward, and the women agree.

records.l: the journey to Marazion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The women plan to leave at 10 A.M. for Marazion by way of Helstone, where they hope to stay for an hour or two. After Charles's proposal, they plan to start at nine, visit the sea-caves, reach Helstone by dinner-time, and arrive at Marazion before dark.

records.l: death, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The narrator reflects that death appears differently to the old, who may see it not as an enemy but as a friend. She imagines death as unable to harm them and possibly able to restore what life has denied or taken away.

records.l: the afterlife, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE EIGHTH And seven days were all we could allow ourselves at the Lizard, if we meant to see the rest of Cornwall.
records.s: The narrator considers the possibility that something within people is imperishable even as the body declines. She expresses faith that death may lead to the Father's care and that more and better things may be given after this life.

records.l: An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: On their last day at the Lizard, the narrator and her children cross Church Cove in John Curgenven's boat to visit Raven's Ugo and Dolor Ugo, while John recounts the rescue of survivors from the emigrant ship Brest. After a difficult landing and a delay caused by a leak in the boat, they travel through Cornwall to Helstone, visiting familiar places and receiving generous hospitality. In Helstone they meet an unnamed Cornish engineer, who warmly welcomes the family connected with his former employers and shares his home, inventions, garden produce, and memories.

records.l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The narrator feels sad to leave the Lizard and apprehensive about crossing the rough, seaweed-covered rocks at Church Cove. She joins the boat trip, listens to John's account of the Brest wreck, visits the caves, and later records her gratitude for John, the laundress, the apple giver, and the Helstone hosts.

records.l: John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: John rows the party to the sea caves and helps them board and leave the boat safely. He recounts rescuing women and children from the Brest wreck, showing a hand with half a finger missing from that rescue, and is described as strong, fearless, chivalrous, careful, honest, and kind.

records.l: chickens (the old hen's chickens), An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The narrator's children cross the slippery rocks and board John's boat, then help with the difficult landing. They later gather apples from a cottage tree and travel with the narrator to Helstone.

records.l: the Cornish engineer, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The Cornish engineer welcomes the narrator's party enthusiastically because of his enduring devotion to her family, for whom he had worked abroad. He describes his engineering work, shows them his inventions and the candle used by an emperor to light a lighthouse, and gives them tea, grapes, and apples.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The Lizard, once merely a name or mark on a map to the travelers, has become associated with living human relationships and memories. The party leaves it sadly after visiting its town, church, coast, and sea caves.

records.l: Church Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: Church Cove is reached after the travelers leave their carriage, and they descend to the shore to board John's boat. Its rough, slippery rocks and advancing waves make both embarkation and landing difficult.

records.l: Raven's Ugo, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: Raven's Ugo is the first cave the party examines from the boat. Its entrance lies above the sea line, is hung with sea-ferns, and has long been occupied by a pair of ravens; in smuggling days it was used to hide kegs of spirits.

records.l: Dolor Ugo, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: Dolor Ugo is a solemn, colorful cave whose floor is entirely heaving, clear, deep olive-green water. Boats can enter as far as the daylight reaches, but its inland extent is unknown because exploring it would require dangerous swimming.

records.l: the Lizard coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The Lizard coast is portrayed as magnificent, gloomy, and iron-bound, with cliffs, sea caves, and a history of wrecks and smuggling. The narrator regrets that the party's boat trip provides its last view of the coast.

records.l: Helstone, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: Helstone is reached after the party travels inland from Gunwalloe. The travelers rest and eat at an old-fashioned inn before finding their unknown friend, the Cornish engineer, who is well known in the town.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: Cornwall is described as having bleak and beautiful downs, old churches, broad local dialects, tidy cottages, generous inhabitants, and persistent horses and men. The narrator associates the region with courage, hospitality, and personal loyalty.

records.l: the boat belonging to John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: John's boat carries the party over very large waves to the sea caves, though the voyage repeatedly rises and falls like a cork on the sea. It has an innocent leak, and the travelers' garments become soaked to the knees before they can be dried at a nearby cottage.

records.l: the emigrant ship Brest, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The Brest went down near the Lizard on a winter night. Its survivors included women and children who were rescued in boats, brought ashore with little clothing, and sheltered by fishermen's cottages and the parsonage.

records.l: shipwrecks along the Cornish coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: Shipwrecks are John's favorite subject and are a recurring feature of the Lizard coast's history. The narrator also hears of wrecks at Gunwalloe, where survivors have been saved from rocks and cargo and other remains have washed ashore.

records.l: the journey from the Lizard to Helstone, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The journey includes the return from Church Cove, drying wet clothes, visits to Mary Mundy, Mullion, and Gunwalloe, and a long inland drive through quiet villages and apple-growing country. The travelers eventually reach Helstone, where they rest and visit the Cornish engineer.

records.l: the planned boat excursion to the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall, " DAY THE NINTH And our last at the Lizard, which a week ago had been to us a mere word or dot in a map; now we carried away from it a living human interest in everything and everybody.
records.s: The boat trip is hazardous because of the heavy waves, rough rocks, and open sea, but John rows confidently and guides the party into Raven's Ugo and Dolor Ugo. The travelers admire the caves, hear about wrecks and smugglers, and become accustomed to the boat's motion.
