records.l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The narrator is a travelling woman and conductor of a Cornwall tour with two young companions, her “chickens.” She values holidays, modest preparation, economy, health, cheerfulness, and attentive enjoyment of scenery and people. Though her feet are feeble, she is steady-minded and protects the chickens from rash adventures and illness. The journey begins in a comfortable carriage from Falmouth toward the Lizard, with Charles; she discusses temperance, hears of his bereavement, and gathers Cornish heath. At Mullion Cove she lets the companions explore a difficult descent while she remains above, then visits a cave, admires the shore and sunset, observes tide-bound visitors, and returns with assistance. She enjoys tea at the Old Inn and notices farmyard animals and moonlight. On Sunday she walks about Lizard, attends church at Landewednack, watches sunset and moonlit country, and sees calm beauty turn into a violent storm, fearing the holiday spoiled. More than a year later, she finishes this account of fifteen innocent days as a memorial of “a good time.”

records.l: chickens (the old hen's chickens), An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The chickens are two young female companions of the narrator, one in her teens and one in her twenties, described as young adventurers and bathers among the narrator's party. Expected to follow instructions, travel lightly, avoid needless risks, and support the group's health and happiness, they repeatedly visit sea-pools and search rocks and little pools for sea-treasures. They gather blackberries for pudding, collect flowers and heaths, and explore the Lizard's cove of sea-weeds and sea-anemones before the tide rises. Later they scramble over Penolver and return enthusiastic about its cliff walk. On the last day, they cross slippery rocks, board John's boat, assist at a difficult landing, gather apples, and travel to Helstone.

records.l: King Arthur, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: King Arthur is a legendary or possibly nonexistent king of Britain, regarded by some as a Cornishman and by others as an ideal knight or noble modern gentleman. Debate over whether he lived is central: practical minds doubt him, while tradition presents him as a figure of goodness and knighthood amid a violent age. He is described as the son of Uther Pendragon and Ygrayne, raised by Sir Ector, proclaimed king after Uther’s death, founder of the Order of Knights of the Round Table, and husband of Queen Guinevere. His story ends at Camelford, where Mordred conquers and grievously wounds him. Arthur orders Sir Bedevere to cast Excalibur into a mere, then sails with three queens to Avillion to be healed. Accounts differ over whether he was buried, remains in fairy land, or will return to Cornwall; he is also believed to revisit Tintagel as a chough, and a mound is identified as his grave.

records.l: the Cornish people, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Cornish people are portrayed as a distinct group reputed to be honest, simple, shrewd, kind, just, faithful, and brave. Though warned they seek favourable terms, the narrator rejects assumptions of cheating. They unfold as courteous, independent people whose rich and poor meet socially and treat strangers kindly.

records.l: Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Cornwall is a county and coastal region of strong Cornish character, ancestry, speech, and traditions: a respectable, sober-minded, religious-minded place whose inhabitants are portrayed as independent, dependable, generous, courageous, hospitable, and loyal. It contains fishing communities, working mining districts, tidy villages and cottages, old churches, quarries, sea-caves, hedge walls, distinctive rocks and plants, grey cows, deep-cut lanes shared with Devon, and a coast shaped by blue seas, cliffs, caves, shipwrecks, coast-guard courage, and danger from the Atlantic. In fine weather its atmosphere is fresh, dry, mild, balmy, and bracing, with clear skies and sunshine; elsewhere the sea, storms, darkness, and increasingly bare western landscape emphasize its wildness and risk. The records unfold as an Unsentimental Journey by three travelers who begin with a long-held wish to investigate Cornwall simply, avoiding fashionable towns where possible and going around the coast. Early days introduce its old, wild country, rough roads, granite, ancient associations, coastal hazards, and legends. At the Lizard, a place initially only a word or map-dot, the party spends seven days and comes to feel a living human interest in everything and everybody. They then continue toward Marazion by way of Helstone, encountering varied gardens, avenues, mining country, villages, broad views, and practical hospitality, with only one complaint of being charged double for milk. As the journey moves westward, Cornwall appears more barren but also peaceful, solitary, and sunlit. Later travel brings railway, wooded country, moorland, slate quarries, and grand sunsets. The final movement enters King Arthur's land, including Tintagel and Camelford: a sparsely inhabited world of ruins, caves, dramatic coast, and dangerous sea, where Arthurian loves, hatreds, virtues, and crimes seem fitted to the rugged landscape. More than a year afterward, the journey remains remembered as a shared passage through Cornwall.

records.l: the Cornish coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a grand, wild, dangerous coast DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.] The Cornish coast is characterized as the grandest, wildest, and most dangerous coast, requiring adventurous travellers to take precautions. The narrator intends to make a circuit around it with her companions.

records.l: Land's End, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Land's End is the extreme western point of the island, at the end of a peninsula, overlooking the Atlantic across a magnificent circle of sea. Long a recurring landscape-dream and desired destination of the narrator's childhood, it becomes the travelers' goal of pilgrimage as they complete their coastal circuit. Reached on a Sunday after a long journey, it proves no disappointment: a grand, lonely, constantly windy place, almost as solitary as a ship at sea and compared to the Great Temple of nature. The party eats at the First and Last Inn, explores the fine cliff-walk scenery, and looks over the rocky coast, including the Armed Knight, the Irish Lady, and the Brisons. Though it attracts tourists in large numbers, the Sunday visit is valued as less crowded. On the following morning, after leaving Whitesand Bay, the companions take a second and final look. The place is also linked by report to landings by Athelstan, King Stephen, King John, and Perkin Warbeck.

records.l: Exeter, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.] Exeter is where the travellers meet and spend the night before beginning their Cornwall tour. The narrator visits its cathedral and old town, then departs from Exeter on 1 September 1881.

records.l: Falmouth, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Falmouth is a place with a sheltered bay and glittering sea beyond. Reached after Plymouth, Saltash, Liskeard, Lostwithiel, and St. Austell, it provides a stay at the Green Bank hotel, arrangements for the Lizard, and the starting point for a carriage journey whose upland road looks back over the town and bay.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Lizard is a Cornish coastal place and sightseeing point, recommended as possibly better than Land's End. It includes Lizard Town with shops, white-painted houses, two nearby hotels, a church, gardens and paths into quieter countryside. Its coast has cliffs, a sparkling sea, serpentine rocks, sea-pools, caves, and a cove reached by a difficult descent. The Lizard Lights, a huge white building and navigational installation, are a prominent feature. It is reputed for exceptionally dense fogs and is noted for longevity: register books record several deaths at more than one hundred years, while a rector is said to have died at 120. The travelers arrange lodgings by telegram, then arrive by carriage after crossing Goonhilly Down. During their stay they make excursions around the cliffs, shore, church connections, and lights; a severe nighttime storm keeps them there while Charles nevertheless brings a party through the weather. After a divine day, they bathe, explore the shore, and visit the lights before preparing for Marazion. What began as only a word or dot on a map becomes a place of human interest, memories, and affection, and they leave sadly after revisiting its town, church, coast, and sea caves.

records.l: travel and rational tourism, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Travel and rational tourism is a deliberate way of seeing places that rejects frantic sight-collecting. It begins with belief in holidays and unfolds by arguing that observing and enjoying matter because the traveller's mind creates travel's real interest.

records.l: the journey through Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A planned but adaptable journey through Cornwall began at Exeter on 1 September 1881, guided by “Hope for the best, and be prepared for the worst.” Its first day brought rail travel, fellow-traveller conversations, Falmouth, and preparations for the Lizard; we three completed it in fifteen days.

records.l: the departure from Exeter, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: occurred_on 1 September 1881 [a lovely September day] DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.] The departure from Exeter takes place on 1 September 1881 in exceptionally fine weather. The travellers watch the landscape from the railway, including the Exe estuary, Dawlish, Plymouth, Saltash, and the country beyond.

records.l: the Land's End circuit, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a planned circuit around Cornwall's coast [ending at Land's End] DAY THE FIRST I believe in holidays.] The Land's End circuit is the narrator's proposed route around the Cornish coast, ending at Land's End. She intends the circuit to allow her and her companions to investigate Cornwall gradually rather than hurry through it.

records.l: obedience to the conductor, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Obedience to the conductor is the narrator’s golden rule of group travel: choose one competent decision-maker, require implicit obedience from the others, and let them coincide throughout the journey.

records.l: economical travel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Economical travel means packing as little as possible, avoiding show and huge hotels, choosing quiet humble lodgings, spending reasonably, and using practical clothing and footwear without needless hardship.

records.l: Cornish character, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Cornish character is associated with justice, common sense, fidelity, bravery, honesty, simplicity, shrewdness, and kindness; the narrator seeks to discover whether these qualities persist among Cornish people.

records.l: Charles, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Charles is a reliable, kindly Cornish carriage driver and guide, employed by a livery-stable keeper and providing carriage and horse for the narrator, her two young companions, and other women travelers. A bright-looking, intelligent young fellow and lifelong teetotaller, he is faithful both to his passengers and to his horse, which he tends carefully and allows rest and feed when journeys demand it. He owns the carriage, knows the Lizard country and regularly visits Mullion Cove with picnic parties. He also carries private grief: he tells the narrator that his wife died after their baby died. From the second day onward, Charles drives the party from Falmouth to the Lizard, collecting heaths, identifying local features, and helping them despite rain and difficult ground. He arranges a boatman, warns them of dangerous sea and landing conditions, points out the Lizard Lights, and guides the narrator along narrow hedge-wall paths. On the third day he arrives early with an elaborate itinerary for Kennack Sands, Poltesco, Cadgwith, and Mullion; he remains alert to comfort, sightseeing, and the horse’s welfare during demanding travel. At Mullion Cove he guides and assists the travelers, helps the narrator through a sea-cave, and organizes their return to the farm and Old Inn before taking the horse toward Falmouth. Even when soaked and hatless after bringing another party to the Lizard in severe weather, Charles appears smiling and sympathetic. When the travelers leave the Lizard, he resumes charge of their journey, adapts routes through Mullion and Gunwalloe to include sea-caves, recommends a Norwegian boatman, and offers help with a moonlit row around St. Michael’s Mount. He explains the decline of Cornwall’s mining industry while showing them disused tin mines. Later he gives the horse an easier day, has the travelers walk heavy hills where appropriate, and offers to gather blackberries while they proceed on foot. On their final day, he offers to take them anywhere despite his overnight return to Falmouth, plans the horse’s rest, and parts mournfully while reassuring them that he often makes the journey.

records.l: Trelowarren, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Trelowarren, seat of the old Cornish Vyvyan family, lies on a route from Falmouth to the Lizard. Travelers begin there on a smiling morning, passing through its woods and ferny glades while its underground chambers and galleries remain unseen.

records.l: Goonhilly Down, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Goonhilly Down, an old Cornish-named hunting ground, is a broad, flat, bare, treeless district. Believed once to have been an enormous forest full of wild beasts, it contains serpentine blocks through the turf. Travelers cross it, gather Cornish heath, and encounter associations with St. Rumon and Goonhillies.

records.l: the Lizard Lights, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Lizard Lights are an early lighthouse experiment: a huge, dazzling-white low building resembling Sydenham Crystal Palace, with a tower at either side. At sunset its two powerful lights, each stated at 20,000 candles, replace the suns and send beams across sea and landscape. They are visible far into darkness from the sea and moonlit countryside, claimed at twenty miles and perhaps thirty, but fog hides them; then a fog-horn sounds. First watched nightly from afar, they become the narrator’s only visible illumination during the storm’s darkest phase and later a familiar yet beautiful sight. On the eighth day, the women visit and see the enormous lamps, ladders, lighting apparatus, and fog-horn machinery, whose workings they cannot understand.

records.l: the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Lizard is a coastal district and region in Cornwall, marked by a sharp geological line of magnesian earth and serpentine blocks in turf, cottage walls, and fences. Its coast has rough seas, difficult landings, steep paths, dangerous rocks, and shipwrecks, with Pistol Meadow and the Lizard Lights. Though subject to dense fogs, it can unfold in clear blue sea, sunshine, bracing air, and villages such as Cadgwith.

records.l: the serpentine, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Serpentine is a reddish and greenish stone found along the coast near the Lizard. It is used for cottage walls, fences, a stile, and polished ornaments and architectural objects, including candlesticks, brooches, mantelpieces, tombstones, and studs. It is the district’s principal commerce; at Poltesco it is fashioned into delicate, sometimes Pompeian forms, while Cadgwith rocks range from red and green to grey.

records.l: the horse, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Charles's horse is a handsome, well-rested animal accustomed to rough roads. Tethered in the ordinary Cornish fashion, it travels lively across the Downs to Mullion and Mullion Cove after resting. Before the return journey toward Falmouth, Charles plans to feed and groom it well.

records.l: the carriage, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The carriage is a comfortable vehicle used for the Lizard journey. Drawn by a horse, it carries the narrator and two young companions from Falmouth at a leisurely pace, stopping for blackberries and heaths. On the next day, Charles drives the women through Lizard Town and the countryside toward Kennack Sands, Poltesco, and Cadgwith, taking an inland route when the cliff route cannot be used.

records.l: the Lizard journey, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Lizard journey is a carriage trip beginning at Falmouth, taking the less regular route through Trelowarren and Goonhilly Down rather than Helstone, and ending at Lizard. Despite arriving late, the travelers enjoy scenery, flowers, geological features, and an unhurried ride.

records.l: the practical narrator's companions, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The narrator's companions are a group of female travellers who share a fifteen-day Cornwall journey with her. Practical and mutually supportive, they place themselves in Charles's care for a day's excursion, are prepared for emergencies, and make wet weather enjoyable with needlework, knitting, reading Idylls of the King and Morte d'Arthur, artwork, and shopping. Their travels include Kennack Sands, Poltesco, Cadgwith, Mullion Cove, Housel Cove, and the Lizard. They collect flowers, explore scenery and local life, help the narrator through a cave, bathe in the Atlantic, sketch near Kynance, and attend tea and church. In rough water, they join the narrator in hiring a boat for an evening row, abandon the plan to reach Kynance Cove, watch the sunset and Lizard Lights, and return safely with Charles and John Curgenven. More than a year later, the journey is remembered as an Unsentimental Journey taken by three companions during fifteen innocent days.

records.l: John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: John Curgenven is an about-sixty-year-old Lizard fisherman and boatman, of Cornish ancestry, who owns and operates a boat for excursions. The elder boatman and stroke-oar, he knows the coast and safely handles his boat near dangerous rocks. He is portrayed as weather-beaten yet refined, with strong arms, a fearless honest face, self-control guided by conscience and common sense, and a bearing likened to King Arthur. Kind to young people and considerate of an old lady, he gives the party fish, offers to take them to Kynance Cove, leads them over the downs, assists them across rough ground, and explains caves, tides, and local dangers. He leaves before the Cove because of another engagement; later, his wife sells the party serpentine. On their final day at the Lizard, he rows them to the sea caves and helps them embark and disembark safely. He recounts rescuing women and children from the Brest wreck, during which a rope took half a finger. He also helps guide the narrator home along hedge walls.

records.l: the coastguard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The coastguard is a group of picked service men, fearless, faithful, steady, and courageous. Accustomed to traveling the coast at all hours, they guide themselves by white-washed rocks on dark nights and help in wreck rescues. Their winter occupation is risky and tolerably well paid, though no money fully compensates for what they endure.

records.l: the fishermen of the Lizard, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The fishermen of the Lizard are generally unpaid or minimally paid volunteers who assist coast-guard men in rescue work when ships wreck, especially when the lifeboat is insufficient. They endure the community’s winter hardship and dangerous winter seas. In the Brest wreck, they rescue survivors, take women and children ashore, and shelter survivors in fishermen’s cottages and the parsonage.

records.l: Kynance Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Kynance Cove is a Cornwall place about two miles beyond Gull Rock and Asparagus Island. The party first considers rowing there but postpones the visit for daylight. On the seventh day, John Curgenven leads them by a path across the downs and a steep descent to its richly colored rocks, Drawing-room, Dining-room, and Kitchen caves, Asparagus Island, the Bellows, and Gull Rock; the advancing tide makes its attractions inaccessible.

records.l: Asparagus Island, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: has_name_origin no asparagus Asparagus Island has no asparagus, despite its name, and can be reached by climbing a path that the narrator considers unsafe for herself. The girls climb it successfully, and the elderly clergyman says that it is easy enough compared with the more dangerous rocks.

records.l: Mount's Bay, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mount's Bay is described as a shallow bay containing St. Michael's Mount. At low tide, a wet, seaweed-covered causeway crosses it to the Mount; at high tide, it becomes a sheet of rippling, moonlit water.

records.l: the Atlantic Ocean, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Atlantic Ocean is a wide, illimitable ocean lying between America with no intervening land. Along the Cornish coast, it sends rollers and heavy ground-swells before storms, making boating and landing dangerous; yet on a divine day it reaches bathers in gentle ripples and invites swimming as far as prudence permits.

records.l: the sea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The sea is a broad natural expanse, bounded by America at the horizon, resembling the Mediterranean in blueness, and visible from Mullion Cove before its inner sandy nook. It surrounds Lizard, contains submerged Lyonesse, and normally sends ground-swell along the coast. It unfolds through changing shore views: first dark, rough, and difficult to cross, with hills, valleys, foaming whirlpools, and beautiful sunset, moonrise, and reflected lights; then rolling over silver sand beneath a setting sun. It becomes calm and brilliantly blue with birds and pools, receives the day’s last glow, and in storm merges with the sky into darkness. Its waves press toward rocks and sandcastles, culminating in a vast, powerful, solitary, continually moving sea at Land's End, with boiling water below the cliffs and a view toward the Atlantic.

records.l: the boat belonging to John Curgenven, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: John Curgenven’s open boat, propelled by a single pair of oars, carries the narrator and companions among the rocks at the Lizard and later over very large waves to the sea caves. Boatmen steer near dangerous whirlpools before returning as darkness approaches. Landing is difficult because of waves and seaweed. After the sea-cave trip, an innocent leak leaves travelers soaked to the knees.

records.l: the sunset, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The sunset occurs over the Atlantic beyond the Land's End, during a boat trip and as watched from nearby cliffs. The sun drops like a red round ball into the sea; after its last light disappears, the Lizard Lights burst out and an unusual green gleam appears, holding two young lovers' attention.

records.l: Pistol Meadow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Pistol Meadow is a green area on the cliff path containing foreign sailors' shipwreck burial place, feared after dark because of graves and stories that other things walk there.

records.l: the shipwreck at Pistol Meadow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: More than a hundred years earlier, a ship went to pieces in the cove below Pistol Meadow; over two hundred foreign sailors were buried there, while only two of seven hundred survived after the captain put them in irons.

records.l: the lifeboat, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_insufficient_for_rescues shipwrecks along the Cornish coast [the volunteers also use their own boats] The lifeboat is kept at the lifeboat house, whose door invites contributions and whose key is held at a nearby house and the Rectory. It is difficult to run down to the beach on a dark winter night and is not considered sufficient by itself for rescue work.

records.l: Cornish hedge walls, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Cornish hedge walls are stone-and-earth walls in the Lizard district, six to ten feet high and about two feet broad, dividing land instead of fences and forcing travelers along narrow, precarious tops.

records.l: shipwrecks along the Cornish coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Shipwrecks are a recurring, often deadly danger along the Cornish coast, particularly at the Lizard and its Stags rocks. In winter, wild storms or dense fogs bring wrecks almost weekly: distress guns sound, lifeboats launch, ships break apart, and notices may report “all hands lost.” The records begin with the coast’s many marked sites of destruction and John’s account of a ship vanishing within ten minutes after striking. They continue with the lighthouse attendant’s repeated winter wrecks at the Lizard, then end with John’s interest in this history and accounts from Gunwalloe, where survivors, cargo, and other wreckage reach shore.

records.l: Arthurian legends, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Arthurian legends are legends centered on King Arthur and associated with Cornwall, Avillion, Lyonesse, Tintagel, Camelford, and beliefs in Arthur’s return or survival in fairy land. They preserve Arthur’s existence despite time and change, while allowing competing accounts of his disappearance, burial, grave, coffin, and the Round Table. Their stories include Ygrayne, Uther Pendragon, King Mark, Tristram, and Iseult, alongside an idealized Arthur and noble knight. They unfold through a legendary region that readers may believe to differing degrees: from Arthur’s birth-place and last battle to traditions of his loss, return, and haunting of the coast. The legends portray a society where might was right and passions brought love and hate, yet sustain ideals of courage, honour, faith, chastity, devotion, service, and love of woman.

records.l: Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Kynance is a coastal place with a cove and rock chambers, accessible at low water, called a kitchen and drawing-room; it is valued for especially perfect natural bathing places. On the third day it cannot be visited because the tide will not suit until Wednesday or Thursday. On the fourth, it lies west along the cliff path from Lizard, visible in moonlight beyond smooth green stretches and steep, hazardous ones. By the eighth day, its waves are heard at midnight and its Devil's Throat is recalled.

records.l: Kennack Sands, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Kennack Sands is a solitary sandy bay on the Cornish coast, with smooth yellow sands, long Atlantic waves, rock shelters used for bathing, and water whose dangers women travelers observe while girls bathe and flowers are gathered.

records.l: Cadgwith, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Cadgwith is a fishing village in a sheltered coastal bend, protected from the dense fogs of the Lizard. Described as pleasant in summer and winter, it has a small fishing station, village inn, mild climate suitable for invalids, and the nearby Devil's Frying-pan as its principal attraction.

records.l: Mullion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_located_in Cornwall Mullion is reached from the Lizard Down and Pradenack Down. The village contains the Old Inn, and Mullion Cove lies about a mile from it.

records.l: Lizard Town, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Lizard Town is a bright little town on the Lizard peninsula, with a post-office, serpentine shops, and two nearby hotels. Its commercial places provide food, drink, clothing, and ornaments. During the travelers’ excursion, they depart through it, later return toward it from Cadgwith, and on the fifth day wade in to seek a shop.

records.l: Poltesco, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: contains the serpentine works at Poltesco [the district's principal industrial site] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] Poltesco contains the principal serpentine works and a pretty valley with a trout-stream and wooden bridge. The women travelers visit its show-room, see objects ranging from mantelpieces to brooches, and leave wishing they could carry away more of the workmanship.

records.l: the Devil's Frying-pan, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Devil's Frying-pan near Cadgwith is a two-acre natural amphitheatre enclosed by a high semicircular cliff. It opens to the sea through a serpentine arch, where waves reach a shingly beach amid jagged rocks and flying seabirds.

records.l: the serpentine works at Poltesco, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: processes serpentine [into ornamental and architectural objects] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The serpentine works at Poltesco employ about a dozen visible workmen and use machinery whose hum mixes with the nearby trout-stream. A workman explains the process and shows the women travelers a range of finely made serpentine goods, including vases, candlesticks, mantelpieces, tombstones, brooches, and studs.

records.l: the girls at Kennack Sands, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A group of girls related to and under the narrator’s care, practical in scrambling clothing and steady-headed at Kennack Sands. On the seventh day they accompany her to Kynance Cove, bathe and are repeatedly knocked down by waves, visit the Bellows, climb Asparagus Island, avoid more dangerous rocks, return safely, and reach Lizard Point along hedge tops.

records.l: bathing in Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is delightful [when it is available] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] Bathing in Cornwall is described as delightful when it can be safely done, generally at low water on a sandy floor near a comfortable cave. The women travelers do not bathe at Kennack Sands, but girls there play in the sea.

records.l: the Atlantic waves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: can_sweep_bathers_off_their_feet bathers [even in calm weather] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The Atlantic waves at Kennack Sands are long and strong, and their recoil can take a person off their feet even in calm weather. Among the rocks and eddies, they pose a serious danger to swimmers.

records.l: the Cornish fishing communities, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: experience the winter hardship of the Cornish coast [with little work, fishing or market access] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The Cornish fishing communities are portrayed as observant but civil, with people commonly greeting and speaking to visitors. Their working people are described as honest, independent, and respectable, while the villages themselves can be quiet and isolated.

records.l: the serpentine industry, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is the one commerce of the district [centered at Poltesco] DAY THE THIRD "And a beautiful day it is, ladies, though it won't do for Kynance.] The serpentine industry is identified as the one commerce of the district, centered at Poltesco. Its market is limited, especially in winter, when there is said to be no market for serpentine.

records.l: the winter hardship of the Lizard community, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The winter hardship of the Cornish coast is seasonal unemployment: poor fishing and no market for serpentine can leave men without earnings for four months, endured through summer savings and stored hay to prevent starvation.

records.l: Mary Mundy, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mary Mundy is the respected, hospitable innkeeper of the Old Inn at Mullion, a Lizard resident known for red cheeks, black eyes, and voluble, kind strong Cornish. She runs the inn, helps raise a young niece with her brother, and keeps a poem and portrait of the Scotch Professor. Away in Helstone when travelers arrive, she returns that evening, warmly feeds them, restores order, and remembers the Professor.

records.l: Mary Mundy's brother, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mary Mundy’s brother is a man who helps manage the household but depends on Mary Mundy. At the Old Inn, he receives travelers during her marketing absence, regrets her absence, and struggles with household and tea arrangements while promising them tea.

records.l: Old Inn, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Old Inn is a praised, comfortable, full house in Mullion, associated with Mary Mundy and the Professor; travelers dine, rest, give their address, receive a warm welcome from Mary and her brother, and are served substantial homemade tea.

records.l: Helstone, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a town [old-fashioned market town in Cornwall] Helstone is reached after the party travels inland from Gunwalloe. The travelers rest and eat at an old-fashioned inn before finding their unknown friend, the Cornish engineer, who is well known in the town.

records.l: Mullion Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mullion Cove, in Cornwall, is reached by a rough road and steep descent; it has a beach, grand serpentine rocks, offshore Mullion Island, and two sea-caves visited before travelers return to the Old Inn.

records.l: St. Michael's Mount, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: St. Michael's Mount is a historic mount in the middle of Mount's Bay, resembling Mont St. Michel and formed by a battlemented rock, castle, chapel, mediaeval fortress, and modern residence. At its foot is a fishing village of about thirty cottages, while an underground tiny continuous-chain railway serves the Mount. By moonlight it appears grand and mysterious, linked to Cormoran as his legendary dwelling place. The St. Aubyn family bought it in 1660 and has inhabited it ever since. Visitors tour its chapel, vault, halls, drawing-room, and school-room, admiring the site despite its many steps, rough causeway, and difficulties of living there. It receives royal visitors, including an expected visit by Princess Frederica of Hanover and Baron Von Pawel-Rammingen, and shines in the setting sun as travelers pass nearby.

records.l: Dozmare Pool, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Dozmare Pool, near St. Neots, is proposed as the mere of King Arthur’s final departure after his death-wound. Though the travelers do not visit it, they imagine a melancholy, ghostly moorland lake, associated in Cornish ghost stories with Tregeagle, spectral hounds, a phantom coach, and unexplained lights.

records.l: the narrator, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The narrator, a mother of six children, travels with girls around the Lizard and Kynance Cove. She balances curiosity and affection with caution: at the Bellows and Asparagus Island she distinguishes sensible bravery from foolhardy risk, warns the girls away from Hell’s Mouth, and leaves before the tide blocks the route. Walking to Lizard Point, she receives news of sickness and death but finds consolation in moonlight. On her final day she is sad to leave, anxious over Church Cove’s slippery rocks, joins a boat trip and cave visit, hears John’s wreck account, and departs grateful for local kindness and companionship.

records.l: Excalibur, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Excalibur is King Arthur’s sword. Near the end of Arthur’s life, Arthur orders Sir Bedevere to throw it into a mere, said to be Dozmare Pool; its return there is associated with Arthur’s final departure.

records.l: the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mullion Cove has two sea-caves: one on the beach and an outer cave accessible only at low water. The narrator passes through the near cave's dark, winding, seaweed-damp passage and emerges into a secluded sandy nook.

records.l: the tide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_rising fast [at Mullion Cove] The tide is rising fast while visitors are in the farther cave. Several people have to wade ashore up to their knees, and the narrator realizes that she and her companions must hurry or wade through the water themselves.

records.l: Mullion Cove's serpentine rocks, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: are_made_of serpentine [grand enclosing rocks] Mullion Cove's grand serpentine rocks enclose the beach and the secluded nook beyond the cave. The rocks form walls around the nook and are also used for serpentine candlesticks at the Old Inn.

records.l: the tea at the Old Inn, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mary Mundy serves the travelers a substantial tea with hot strong tea, a large home-baked loaf, rich yellow butter, cream, clotted cream, jam, and marmalade. She repeatedly urges them to have more and charges little for the meal.

records.l: Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Landewednack is a parish containing the comparatively modern Lizard Town. On the journey’s fourth day it is the narrator’s destination for an afternoon church visit; its name is said to mean the white-roofed church of St. Wednack in ancient Cornish. By the fifth day it prepares for a harvest festival, with ticketed tea in the rectory garden and an evening thanksgiving service. Its rectors reportedly included one who died aged 120 in 1683.

records.l: the church of Landewednack, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The church of Landewednack, near Lizard Town and close to the sea, is described as England’s most southerly church. Picturesque and carefully maintained, it combines older features, a Norman doorway and curious hagioscope, with a modern serpentine memorial pulpit and neat churchyard. On the fourth day of travel it is noted for its history and notably good choir; by the sixth, the crowded evening service, beautiful music, and rich flowers and fruit make an especially impressive conclusion.
records.t: The church of Landewednack, near Lizard Town and close to the sea, is described as England’s most southerly church. Picturesque and carefully maintained, it combines older features—a Norman doorway and curious hagioscope—with a modern serpentine memorial pulpit and neat churchyard. On the fourth day of travel it is noted for its history and notably good choir; by the sixth, the crowded evening service, beautiful music, and rich flowers and fruit make an especially impressive conclusion.

records.l: the Lizard storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Lizard storm is an especially awful Cornwall storm of torrential rain and howling wind. Beginning on the fourth day after clear, silent skies, it brings an extraordinary deluge and shrieking wind, convincing the narrator that the weather has broken.

records.l: the harvest festival, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: includes the evening thanksgiving service [after tea in the rectory garden] The harvest festival is scheduled for the day after the storm and includes tea in the rectory garden followed by an evening thanksgiving service. The text questions how thankful the festival can seem to farmers after such damaging weather.

records.l: Sunday, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Sunday is a day of rest, Sabbatic peace, and rejoicing. It unfolds first in calm beauty: a cliff walk, morning churchgoing, sunset, and moonlit scenery, before a night storm sharply changes the mood. Later, quiet roads near Land’s End are nearly empty as local people go to church or school; despite guilt about traveling during church hours, the narrator finds deep peace and believes Sunday can be kept outside church doors.

records.l: the storm, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The storm begins at night, obscuring the sea with torrential rain. On the fourth day, rain and wind turn sea and sky into indistinguishable blackness, hiding moon and stars, and continue until dawn. On the fifth day it gradually abates; by sunset wind and rain stop, though flooded lanes and an angry sea remain.

records.l: the evening church service, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The evening church service fills every seat, with chanting, hymns, a harvest anthem, organ music, expressive prayers, a good sermon, and a brilliant closing voluntary.

records.l: the holiday in Cornwall, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_affected_by the Lizard storm [the weather breaks after four days] The holiday in Cornwall has lasted only four days when the weather breaks. The narrator laments that the storm may spoil the holiday, as well as the planned harvest festival.

records.l: the fire, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a fire [the first fire of the season] The travelers decide that they must have a fire, which requires removing their sea-holly and ferns and causes concern for their handmaiden. After initially filling the room with smoke, the fire burns properly and makes the room warm, bright, and comfortable.

records.l: the rain, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a down-pour [even and very heavy] The rain falls heavily throughout most of the day, making the road to Lizard Town literally swimable and leaving the travelers wading through it. It abates somewhat in the afternoon and ceases by sunset.

records.l: Housel Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Housel Cove is an Atlantic-coast cove and secluded bathing place with soft sand and a beautiful serpentine-rock dressing-room. On the sixth day, the narrator and companions spend a divine morning bathing there without organized amusement. On the eighth day, the women return through the fields and again find the bathing delightful.

records.l: Idylls of the King, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: contains The Passing of Arthur [as its concluding section] The travelers read the Idylls of the King all the way through, ending with The Passing of Arthur. Its account of Sir Bedivere throwing Excalibur into the mere deeply moves one of the travelers and prompts a debate about ideals and belief.

records.l: the ideal man, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_impossible ideal [as a conception] The travelers discuss whether it is better to believe in an impossible ideal man than to accept and worship a worldly, mean, or base ideal. The question leads to a long and heated argument.

records.l: Cornish coast-life, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Cornish coast-life in winter commonly brings rain, storms, and fogs, with little frost or snow; a storm during the journey shows the travelers what this life is like throughout the season.

records.l: Lizard Point, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a grand rock Lizard Point is a grand rock reached by the girls through a route mainly along the tops of hedges. The narrator and the girls walk there in the evening and watch a fine sunset.

records.l: the laws of the universe, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: must_be_carried_out at any cost [even to individuals or nations] The laws of the universe must be carried out, even when doing so causes suffering to individuals or nations. Their operation remains connected with mysteries that the text says are not explained.

records.l: the mystery of sorrow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: remains forever unexplained The mystery of sorrow, like the greater mystery of evil, remains unexplained. The text nevertheless affirms that the world can be made marvelously beautiful despite sorrow and even after a day when it seems hardly worth living in.

records.l: DAY THE SIXTH, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: DAY THE SIXTH is a perfect autumn morning and day, cloudless and calm, spent bathing, sketching, attending rectory tea and church, then walking beneath moonlight.

records.l: the rectory tea, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: brings_together rich and poor [for courtesy rather than charity] The rectory tea brings together humble parishioners, elderly people, county families, and other guests. It takes place in a flower-filled garden with tea tables, lawn-tennis on sea-sand, and music from the village wind band before the congregation goes to church.

records.l: the village wind band, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The village wind band, about six wind instruments played by village musicians, performs determinedly flat with a loud, irregular bass. Compared aspirationally with the Philharmonic and Crystal Palace orchestra, it plays at the rectory tea and near hotels, drives listeners away, and ends with “God save the Queen.”

records.l: the elderly clergyman, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: An elderly, expressive clergyman and father who values reasonable activity but despises foolhardy bravado. On the sands, he warns two young people away from a dangerous route near Devil's Throat, notes that his daughters are safely climbing Asparagus Rock, discusses his views with the narrator, and becomes a friendly companion for a time.

records.l: Drawing-room Cave, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a cave [the loveliest at Kynance] The Drawing-room Cave is described as the loveliest of the caves at Kynance Cove, with a floor of soft sand. The narrator and the girls retreat there after bathing, but waves soon begin to cover its floor as the tide comes in.

records.l: the Bellows, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a rock fissure [producing a spout and roar in certain tide conditions] The Bellows is a curious feature at Kynance Cove where, under certain tidal conditions, water forces itself through a narrow fissure in the rock with a loud roar. The narrator visits it with the girls and watches for the largest spout.

records.l: Devil's Throat, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Devil's Throat, also called Hell's Mouth, is a dangerous rock passage requiring a jump over boiling waves. John Curgenven identifies it as a place visitors should not attempt; despite an elderly clergyman's warning, two young people crawl toward its fissure and cave.

records.l: Hell's Mouth, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_dangerous dangerous rock passage Hell's Mouth is another name given for the dangerous place John Curgenven warns the party not to attempt. The narrator repeats his warning to the girls and is relieved that they do not try it.

records.l: the narrator and traveling party, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A traveling party on a Cornish tour, accompanied by Charles as carriage driver, moves through the Lizard, Marazion, Penzance, St. Ives, Land's End, and Whitesand Bay. Their chief goal is Land's End, a lifelong desire reached on a quiet Sunday after travel from Penzance and a visit to the Logan Rock. Before that, they spend their last Lizard day bathing, observing a solar rainbow, touring the Lizard Lights, and hearing wreck accounts; they also take an open-boat bath near Marazion and visit St. Michael's Mount. They admire scenery and associations but dislike Marazion's beach and St. Ives. At Land's End they explore cliffs with a sailor guide and hear local stories. Preferring terra firma to a mine, they return to Whitesand Bay for shell collecting, revisit Land's End, return to Penzance, and arrange departure.

records.l: the tide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The tide comes in quickly at Kynance Cove, covering the sandy floor of Drawing-room Cave by noon and turning a visitor’s rock into an island. The narrator’s party leaves before the route is impassable, while newly arrived tourists are isolated and may need to wade or swim ashore.

records.l: Penolver, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a headland [fine and green] Penolver appears as a fine headland near Housel Cove. The clerical friend's daughters climb over it, and the young folks later go there for a scramble.

records.l: Marazion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Marazion is a quiet town opposite St. Michael's Mount, reached from its shore, with a name linked to Mara-Zion, Jewish colonists, and Phoenician tin trading. Chosen as the women's next resting-place for its history, position, and promised comfort, it first appears after a gorgeous sunset as a picturesque-named but extremely commonplace little town. Its warm welcome and comfortable, home-like old-fashioned inn secure their stay. Though a mild little station, it proves unsuitable for bathing: the small beach is ugly, fishy-smelling, crowded, and covered by dirty shallow water. After visiting the Mount, the travelers leave for St. Ives. Later, the town gathers at beach and station for Princess Frederica of Hanover's expected arrival, watching boats head toward the Mount and speculating about the party.

records.l: Penzance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Penzance is a genteel, extremely civilised town in Cornwall, connected to Falmouth by a good but lonely road. Travelers pass through, preferring Marazion because Penzance seems too genteel despite lovely, richly vegetated surroundings and coastal views. They later return in the evening to arrange departure, discuss a Marazion house, and prepare Charles’s drive to Falmouth.

records.l: Church Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a cove [landing place for the boat trip] Church Cove is reached after the travelers leave their carriage, and they descend to the shore to board John's boat. Its rough, slippery rocks and advancing waves make both embarkation and landing difficult.

records.l: the clerical friend of Kynance, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The clerical friend tells the women that his children have bathed near Kynance, walked to Cadgwith, and gone launce-fishing by moonlight. He explains how launce-fishing is performed and says his children returned home about two o'clock in the morning.

records.l: the lighthouse attendant, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A young, intelligent lighthouse attendant of working-man status, sickly-faced and coughing, guides women through the Lizard Lights, explains its instruments, and recounts wrecks he has witnessed during their limited visit.

records.l: Sir Launcelot, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a bravest knight of King Arthur [and dearest friend] Sir Launcelot is described as King Arthur’s bravest knight and dearest friend. He is the man for whose love Queen Guinevere forsakes Arthur.

records.l: launce-fishing, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a sport [a popular Lizard pastime practiced on moonlight nights] Launce-fishing is described as a popular Lizard pastime carried out on moonlit nights. Participants stand barefoot on wet sand, use a crooked iron spear to hook sand-eels, and may cook their catch over a fire around midnight.

records.l: the launce, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The launce is a sand-eel peculiar to the Cornish coasts. It swims during the day, then at night burrows in sand above the waterline, where moonlight reveals its silvery gleam.

records.l: the perfect solar rainbow, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a luminous circle around the sun [with faint prismatic tints and extending over half the sky] The women see a rare perfect solar rainbow after bathing at Housel Cove. It forms a luminous circle around the sun, changes from yellow to faint prismatic colors, and gradually disappears.

records.l: the lighthouse built by the Cornish engineer, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: produces light [nightly, equal to about 30,000 candles] The lighthouse at the Lizard is represented by the huge white building containing the enormous light and fog-horn apparatus. Its purpose is to help save ships and lives along a dangerous coast.

records.l: the lighthouse machinery, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: operates the fog-horn [through complicated mechanisms] The lighthouse machinery includes Brobdingnagian lamps, devices for producing the light, and complicated mechanisms for keeping the fog-horn working when the light becomes invisible. The light is said to equal about 30,000 candles.

records.l: the planned boat excursion to the sea-caves, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A planned boat excursion to the sea-caves is proposed after earlier boating plans with John Curgenven fail. With little time left at the Lizard, Charles suggests taking a boat from Church Cove before the party drives onward, and the women agree. The voyage unfolds in small open boats on rough, hazardous water, amid heavy waves, rocks, cliffs, and open sea. John rows confidently and takes the party into Raven's Ugo and Dolor Ugo, where they admire the caves and hear of wrecks and smugglers. In another rough-water passage from Porth Hern, two boatmen guide the party past cliffs and a slate quarry into a dark cave; fear and awe give way to daylight and sunshine on the return.

records.l: the journey to Marazion, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The women plan to leave at 10 A.M. for Marazion by way of Helstone, where they hope to stay for an hour or two. After Charles's proposal, they plan to start at nine, visit the sea-caves, reach Helstone by dinner-time, and arrive at Marazion before dark.

records.l: death, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a friend [for the old and spiritually prepared] The narrator reflects that death appears differently to the old, who may see it not as an enemy but as a friend. She imagines death as unable to harm them and possibly able to restore what life has denied or taken away.

records.l: the afterlife, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a eternal life [believed to be a possible blessing beyond death] The narrator considers the possibility that something within people is imperishable even as the body declines. She expresses faith that death may lead to the Father's care and that more and better things may be given after this life.

records.l: the Cornish engineer, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Cornish engineer is a clever, highly reliable mechanical engineer whose conscientiousness, probity, and fidelity are valued by employers and by the family he once served abroad. Young in Brazil, he worked for a gold-mining company, later superintended engineering projects, and built a lighthouse with sole charge. In later life he warmly welcomes the narrator’s party, displays inventions, preserves the Emperor’s candle as a relic, and offers hospitality.

records.l: Raven's Ugo, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Raven's Ugo is a sea cave, first examined by a party from a boat on their last day at the Lizard. Above the sea line and hung with sea-ferns, its entrance is occupied by a pair of ravens; formerly, smugglers hid kegs of spirits there.

records.l: Dolor Ugo, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Dolor Ugo is an inaccessible, unusable sea cave, solemn and colorful, with a floor entirely of clear, deep olive-green heaving water. Boats can enter only to the daylight’s reach; beyond that, its extent remains unknown because exploration would require dangerous swimming.

records.l: the Lizard coast, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a iron-bound coast [marked by great gloomy cliffs] The Lizard coast is portrayed as magnificent, gloomy, and iron-bound, with cliffs, sea caves, and a history of wrecks and smuggling. The narrator regrets that the party's boat trip provides its last view of the coast.

records.l: the emigrant ship Brest, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: was_lost_in shipwrecks on the Lizard coast [during a winter night] The Brest went down near the Lizard on a winter night. Its survivors included women and children who were rescued in boats, brought ashore with little clothing, and sheltered by fishermen's cottages and the parsonage.

records.l: the journey from the Lizard to Helstone, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a inland carriage journey [over bleak and beautiful country] The journey includes the return from Church Cove, drying wet clothes, visits to Mary Mundy, Mullion, and Gunwalloe, and a long inland drive through quiet villages and apple-growing country. The travelers eventually reach Helstone, where they rest and visit the Cornish engineer.

records.l: the landing at Church Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: has_condition slippery sea-weedy rocks [between advancing waves] Landing at Church Cove requires a leap from the boat onto slippery, seaweed-covered rocks between the waves. The narrator watches her children land first and is relieved when she herself reaches firm ground.

records.l: Cornish hospitality, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Cornish hospitality is shown on the Lizard through fishermen rescuing and sheltering Brest survivors, a laundress warming travelers, an apple seller's generosity, and a Helstone couple's lavish tea and fruit. Beginning as a mere map dot, the Lizard gains living human interest through repeated help whose givers often refuse payment or thanks.

records.l: personal fidelity, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a passionate personal loyalty [shown by the Cornish engineer toward his former employers' family] Personal fidelity is embodied by the Cornish engineer's lasting devotion to the family of those who employed him. He preserves their likenesses, remembers their kindness, keeps the emperor's lighthouse-lighting candle, and declares that he would travel anywhere to serve them.

records.l: Loe Pool, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Loe Pool is a small lake near Helstone, separated from the sea by a sandbar. Supposedly formed by Tregeagle, it is periodically ceremonially cut through by the Mayor of Helstone so fresh and salt waters meet; travelers discussed but did not visit it.

records.l: moonlit row around St. Michael's Mount, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a row [at night, in moonlight] The travelers undertake a moonlit row around St. Michael's Mount after Charles suggests it. The mild air and shimmering water transform the ordinary town and the Mount into a dreamlike, almost fairy-tale scene, allowing the travelers to imagine the area's legends and history.

records.l: St. Ives, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: St. Ives is a town with dark, narrow, fish-smelling streets, a pilchard fishery, a Town Hall, and Tregenna, an ancient mansion made into an hotel. Travelers reach it by a beautiful but inconvenient road, dislike it and its meal, are shown around by a friendly elderly local man, and hurry back toward Penzance.

records.l: Queen Guinevere, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Queen Guinevere, daughter of King Leodegrance and wife of King Arthur, loves Sir Launcelot to the detriment of her marriage. She forsakes Arthur for Launcelot; tradition says her body was found with Arthur’s at Winchester.

records.l: Sennen, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Sennen is a pretty village with cottages, lodgings, a new schoolhouse, and the ancient parish church St. Sennen's. It is linked to a long-deceased curate whose son the traveling party meets at Land's End. After seeing lights on St. Sennen's in darkness, the party passes through the village in heavy rain; the narrator then encounters local residents and schoolchildren, highlighting schooling amid illiteracy.

records.l: the Logan Rock, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Logan Rock is a massive rocking stone near Treryn, regarded as England’s most remarkable specimen and celebrated since the narrator’s childhood. In 1824 Lieutenant Goldsmith displaced it and was forced to replace it. Though visitors later seek its motion with a guide, it no longer rocks properly.

records.l: the guide, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A solemn Cornish-born sailor-guide, formerly a man-of-war’s-man, leads visitors across fields to the Logan Rock and safely along Land’s End’s perilous rocks. He recounts shipwrecks, Royal Navy service aboard H.M.S. Agamemnon, and Balaklava, then gives the narrator a glittering stone.

records.l: Whitesand Bay, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Whitesand Bay is a wide, sunny sweep of fine sand with minute, varied shells, bright sea, and shallow-looking water. Revisited on a clear Monday for bazaar shells, it delights companions, though an old woman warns bathing may be unsafe from quicksands.

records.l: the Land's End journey, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a fulfilled lifelong desire [with no disappointment in the reality] The Land's End journey fulfills a wish the narrator and traveling party have held for many years. They see the Logan Rock and the cliffs, meet local people, and experience the grandeur of the coast, though rain prevents them from fully visiting Whitesand Bay and other planned sights.

records.l: Botallack Mine, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a Cornish mine Botallack Mine is one of several places the narrator and her companions are told they must see, especially by those with scientific interests. They decide not to visit it, partly because they prefer the coast and partly because they do not wish to descend into a mine.

records.l: shell collecting, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a fascination [for the travellers] The companions collect very small shells at Whitesand Bay, some no larger than a grain of rice or a pin's head. The narrator considers the beach's shells exceptionally beautiful and becomes more absorbed in their delicate perfection than in the historical figures associated with the coast.

records.l: Princess Frederica of Hanover, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Princess Frederica of Hanover, a young half-English, half-foreign princess, marries her father’s secretary, Baron Von Pawel-Rammingen; public fascination follows their romance, then sadness after their infant’s funeral, before their expected visit to St. Michael’s Mount.

records.l: the royal visit to St. Michael's Mount, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_hosted_by the St. Aubyns [as a visit to their residence] The royal visit draws much of Marazion to the beach and leads people to follow the visitors' boats at a respectful distance. The crowd speculates about which person is the princess, how the St. Aubyns will receive the party, and whether the visitors will tour Land's End.

records.l: the journey from Penzance to Falmouth, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a long and lonely drive [undertaken at night] The journey from Penzance to Falmouth is planned for the middle of the night, after the horse has rested. Charles expects the road to be good but lonely, and intends to use the old moon after one o'clock to reach Falmouth by daylight.

records.l: Tintagel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Tintagel is a natural-artificial fortress on a rocky sea promontory, identified as King Arthur’s legendary birthplace and as a castle associated with Ygrayne and the duke of Cornwall. It is also presented as the home of King Mark, Sir Tristram, and Iseult of Ireland. Approached through lonely country, its black rock and surrounding sea are seen at sunset. Travelers visit its decaying ruins, climb its rocks, and find a chapel and spring atop the rock, experiencing a place poised between legend and recorded history.

records.l: Camelford, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Camelford is a respectable, commonplace little town with shops, an inn, and private houses. It is chiefly associated in legend with King Arthur’s last battle, though it is not presented as Camelot. Travelers pass from the town to the River Camel and Slaughter Bridge, said to mark Arthur’s army’s defeat and his death-wound.

records.l: King Uther Pendragon, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: King Uther Pendragon is king of Britain. He falls in love with Ygrayne, besieges her and her husband in Tintagel and Terrabil, has her husband killed, and marries her. After Uther’s death, their son Arthur is proclaimed king in his stead.

records.l: Ygrayne, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Ygrayne, a hapless woman in the Arthurian legends, is first the duke of Cornwall’s wife. King Uther Pendragon falls in love with her; after her husband is slain, she marries Uther, bears Arthur, and later recognizes him when he is proclaimed king.

records.l: the Order of Knights of the Round Table, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a order of knights [dedicated to punishing vice and rescuing oppressed virtue] The Order of Knights of the Round Table is instituted by King Arthur. Its members are expected to travel everywhere, punish vice, and rescue oppressed virtue for the love of God and a noble lady.

records.l: Knights of the Round Table, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Knights of the Round Table serve as Arthur’s order of wandering defenders. One by one, Arthur’s best knights are said to fall away into sin.

records.l: Mordred, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Mordred, King Arthur’s nephew, raises a rebellion against Arthur, fights him at Camelford, and conquers him.

records.l: the Round Table, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The Round Table is associated with the order of knights instituted by King Arthur. The text says that the Round Table, like Arthur’s coffin, is preserved at Winchester.

records.l: Delabole quarries, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Delabole quarries are a stark industrial world of enormous slate masses and debris heaps, worked since Queen Elizabeth’s time. In the region of Tintagel and Camelford, wagons, horses, and steam engines sustain wholesome labor, producing slate for nearby houses, walls, gates, and fences.

records.l: Trevena, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a village [small and quiet despite tourists] Trevena is described as a small village with one street, two inns, and a picturesque old post-office. Despite the increasing number of tourists, it retains a simple and home-like character.

records.l: Tintagel Castle, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Tintagel Castle is a landmark between legend and actual history, made of two castles, one in the sea and one on mainland heights, joined by a narrow causeway. In the travelers’ first view, its steep, dangerous appearance in fast-coming twilight keeps them on nearby cliffs and fields. Its ruins include a prehistoric-looking bastion and gateway, later remains, a spring, chapel, and small burial-ground. Its history is uncertain, possibly linked to Arthur, King Mark, or Castle Terrabil, while winds, waves, and the sea continually erode and divide it.
records.t: Tintagel Castle is a landmark between legend and actual history, made of two castles—one in the sea and one on mainland heights—joined by a narrow causeway. In the travelers’ first view, its steep, dangerous appearance in fast-coming twilight keeps them on nearby cliffs and fields. Its ruins include a prehistoric-looking bastion and gateway, later remains, a spring, chapel, and small burial-ground. Its history is uncertain, possibly linked to Arthur, King Mark, or Castle Terrabil, while winds, waves, and the sea continually erode and divide it.

records.l: the sunset at Tintagel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The sunset at Tintagel unfolds over black foreground rock and the sea covering vanished Lyonesse beneath an amber sky barred with long clouds. A low boat-shaped cloud seems to carry three figures, imagined as King Arthur and the three queens, before the travelers joke that the dark shape at its bow is Arthur’s luggage.

records.l: Bossinney Cove, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Bossinney Cove is a pleasant, shut-in cove, visited three times daily by an old sand-collecting man and his eleven named donkeys. During Arthurian days, the narrator and companions bathe there, remembering its steep dangerous path, secluded water, and patient man and animals.

records.l: Boscastle, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a village [built at the end of a deep narrow creek] Boscastle is described as a picturesque village at the end of a deep, narrow creek that shelters sizable vessels. Its surroundings include headlands, the remains of Bottrieux Castle, Ferrabury Church, a blow-hole, and a legend about church bells lost at sea.

records.l: Porth Hern, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Porth Hern, the iron gate opposite Tintagel, receives a rocky stream from Trevena; across Arthurian days, the narrator and companions depart there by boat to visit sea-caves beyond Tintagel.

records.l: sea-cave beyond Tintagel, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A dark, narrow, dangerous sea-cave beyond Tintagel, reached by boat from Porth Hern through stormy water and towering cliffs; its confined waves and tunnel-like darkness inspire terror and intense beauty, ending in the narrator’s vivid but incomplete memory.

records.l: Arthurian chivalry, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: Arthurian chivalry is an ideal that begins by enjoining courage, honour, and chivalrous love of woman, and unfolds as faith, chastity, worship of God, service to humanity, reverence for women, conscience, redressing wrongs, avoiding slander, and fidelity.

records.l: L'ENVOI, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_published_in London L'ENVOI Written more than a year after.] L'ENVOI was written more than a year after the events described. It concludes the history of the journey and is followed by the statement "THE END."

records.l: history of the fifteen innocent days, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: A history of the fifteen innocent days, ending in December fog after recounting the group's calm, bright journey through Cornwall.

records.l: the fifteen innocent days, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: The fifteen innocent days were calm and bright, unfolding as we three took an Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall.

records.l: a good time, An Unsentimental Journey through Cornwall
records.s: is_a memorial [simple] L'ENVOI Written more than a year after.] "A good time" is how Americans would call the experience memorialized by the writer. Its sunshine may cast brightness far forward, even into the quiet time "when travelling days are done."

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Dr. Jessie MacGregor specializes in pathology (described as splendid)
records.q: Miss MacGregor was one of the J.-B. lot, and she and I had awful rows over that question. But we certainly got on very well before that, and, as she says, that was not a personal question. I am quite sure Miss MacGregor is Scotch enough not to propose any arrangement which won’t be to her own advantage. Probably, I know a good many more people than she does. The question for me is whether it will be for my advantage. I am rather inclined to think it will. Miss MacGregor is a splendid pathologist.

records.s: University of Edinburgh opens its doors to women doctors (under a new Head)

records.s: Elsie Inglis serves on Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association (as Vice-President)

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Elsie Inglis leaves the Liberal Party (to advance women’s causes independently)

records.q: In 1901 she was a member of the Women’s Liberal League, a branch of the W.L.A. which split off at the time of the Boer War, in opposition to the ‘Little Englanders.’ Dr. Inglis was on its first committee, and lent her drawing-room for meetings, addressing other meetings on the Imperialist doctrines born in that war.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Dr. Inglis's last message requests support for Serbia (through hospitals and transport)
records.q: Will send Gwynn in a day or two with explanations and suggestions. Colonel Miliantinovitch and Colonel Tcholah Antitch were to make appointment this week or next from Winchester; do see them, and also as many of the committee as possible and show them every hospitality. They have been very kind to us, and whatever happens, dear Miss Palliser, do beg the Committee to make sure that they (the Serbs) have their hospitals and transport, for they do need them.
records.t:

Will send Gwynn in a day or two with explanations and suggestions. Colonel Miliantinovitch and Colonel Tcholah Antitch were to make appointment this week or next from Winchester; do see them, and also as many of the committee as possible and show them every hospitality. They have been very kind to us, and whatever happens, dear Miss Palliser, do beg the Committee to make sure that they (the Serbs) have their hospitals and transport, for they do need them.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Elsie Inglis has a strong sense of equal justice (formed under her father’s influence)
records.q: Through it all Elsie was living in the presence chamber of her father’s chivalrous, high-minded outlook. Whatever action she took then, must have had his approval, and it was from him that she received that keen sense of equal justice for all.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Elsie Inglis differs with Dr. Jex Blake (over the management of the school)
records.q: Here Elsie was with her father, and carried on her studies from his house. It was not an altogether happy start, and very soon she had occasion to differ profoundly with Dr. Jex Blake in her management of the school.

Elsie Inglis differs with Dr. Jex Blake (over the management of the school), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
Here Elsie was with her father, and carried on her studies from his house. It was not an altogether happy start, and very soon she had occasion to differ profoundly with Dr. Jex Blake in her management of the school.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Elsie Inglis is encouraging toward Medical College for Women, Edinburgh (through its difficult early period)
records.q: When I myself began to study medicine, no one could have been more enthusiastically encouraging, and even through the stormy and somewhat depressing times of the early career of the Medical College for Women, Edinburgh, her faith and vision never faltered, and she helped us all to hold on courageously.
records.t:

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Sir William MacEwan achieves a worthy name (in the profession)
records.q: The now Sir William MacEwan enjoyed the fight quite as much as his women students; and if to-day he notes the achievements of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, he may count as his own some of their success in the profession in which he has achieved so worthy a name.

records.s: Glasgow Infirmary Managers oppose mixed classes (in the Infirmary)
records.q: Those old wretches, the Infirmary Managers, have reared their heads again, and now have decided that we are not to go to mixed classes

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Dr. T. opposes mixed classes (at the Glasgow Infirmary)
records.q: So he hummed and hawed, looked everywhere except at us, and then said the Infirmary Managers said we were not to go to mixed classes.
records.t:
Dr. T. opposes mixed classes (at the Glasgow Infirmary), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
So he hummed and hawed, looked everywhere except at us, and then said the Infirmary Managers said we were not to go to mixed classes.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Dr. T. threatens women students' campaign for mixed classes (with physical force)
records.q: True, the baffled and puzzled enemy often played into their hands, as when Dr. T., driven to extremity in a weak moment, threatened to prevent their attendance by ‘physical force.’
records.t:
Dr. T. threatens women students' campaign for mixed classes (with physical force), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: women students' campaign for mixed classes wins mixed classes (after a prolonged dispute at the Glasgow Infirmary)
records.q: The dispute went on until at length an exhausted foe laid down its weapons, and the redoubtable Dr. T. conveyed the intimation that the women students might go to any of the classes--and a benison on them!
records.t:
women students' campaign for mixed classes wins mixed classes (after a prolonged dispute at the Glasgow Infirmary), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
The dispute went on until at length an exhausted foe laid down its weapons, and the redoubtable Dr. T. conveyed the intimation that the women students might go to any of the classes--and a benison on them!

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: mixed classes is supported by University Commissioners (through the draft ordinance)
records.q: This was the draft ordinance of the Commissioners which actually put the education of women on the same footing as that of men, and, worse still, seemed to countenance mixed classes.

mixed classes is supported by University Commissioners (through the draft ordinance), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis

records.s: Sir William Muir supports medical education (as an ally of the campaign)

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: New Hospital for Women is located in Euston Road (London)
records.q: After completing her clinical work in Glasgow, and passing the examination for the Triple Qualification in 1892, it was decided that Elsie should go to London and work as house-surgeon in the new Hospital for Women in the Euston Road.
records.t:
New Hospital for Women is located in Euston Road (London), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
After completing her clinical work in Glasgow, and passing the examination for the Triple Qualification in 1892, it was decided that Elsie should go to London and work as house-surgeon in the new Hospital for Women in the Euston Road.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: New Hospital for Women has been established for nearly thirty years (when Elsie Inglis began working there)
records.q: In 1916 that hospital kept its jubilee year, and when Elsie went to work there it had been established for nearly thirty years.

New Hospital for Women has been established for nearly thirty years (when Elsie Inglis began working there), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
