records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: New Hospital for Women has four wards (including two round wards and two oblong wards)
records.q: There are four wards, two of them round, with two fireplaces back to back in the middle. The other two wards are oblong, and they are all prettily painted, and bright.
records.t:
New Hospital for Women has four wards (including two round wards and two oblong wards), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
There are four wards, two of them round, with two fireplaces back to back in the middle. The other two wards are oblong, and they are all prettily painted, and bright.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: New Hospital for Women has out-patient department (with comfortable and attractive waiting rooms)
records.q: You never saw such a splendid out-patient department as they have here--a perfectly lovely, comfortable waiting-room, and pretty receiving waiting-room.
records.t:
New Hospital for Women has out-patient department (with comfortable and attractive waiting rooms), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
You never saw such a splendid out-patient department as they have here--a perfectly lovely, comfortable waiting-room, and pretty receiving waiting-room.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: New Hospital for Women receives patients (in a paying out-patient department)
records.q: The patients have to pay a small sum, yet they had over 20,000 visits this year up to November--that is about half the size of the Glasgow Royal, one of the biggest out-patients in the kingdom, and general.
records.t:
New Hospital for Women receives patients (in a paying out-patient department), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
The patients have to pay a small sum, yet they had over 20,000 visits this year up to November--that is about half the size of the Glasgow Royal, one of the biggest out-patients in the kingdom, and general.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: New Hospital for Women is staffed by women doctors (including Garrett Anderson and Mrs. Scharlieb)
records.q: Just twenty-one years before the war broke down the last of the barriers against women’s work as doctors, Elsie Inglis entered the New Hospital for Women, to learn with that staff of women doctors who had achieved so much under conditions so full of difficulties and discouragements.

records.s: Mrs. Scharlieb is about forty (dark and solemn in appearance)

records.t:

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: London is a city (the setting of Elsie Inglis’s hospital work and wider activities)
records.q: In the active months of her residence she resolutely ‘tramped’ London, attended most of the outstanding churches, and was a great sermon taster of ministers ranging from Boyd Carpenter to Father Maturin.
records.t:
London is a city (the setting of Elsie Inglis’s hospital work and wider activities), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
In the active months of her residence she resolutely ‘tramped’ London, attended most of the outstanding churches, and was a great sermon taster of ministers ranging from Boyd Carpenter to Father Maturin.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: women doctors practise medical practice (as a new and contested professional principle)
records.q: The hearts of many present went over the washing seas, to the lands wasted by fire and sword, and to the leader of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, who had gained her earliest surgical experience in the wards of the first hospital founded by the first woman doctor, and standing for the new principle that women can practise the healing art.
records.t:
women doctors practise medical practice (as a new and contested professional principle), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
The hearts of many present went over the washing seas, to the lands wasted by fire and sword, and to the leader of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, who had gained her earliest surgical experience in the wards of the first hospital founded by the first woman doctor, and standing for the new principle that women can practise the healing art.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: women doctors are excluded from medical societies (despite their qualifications and hospital work)
records.q: And that man, you know, can be a fellow of the colleges, and member of any society he likes to apply to, while Mrs. G. Anderson and Mrs. Scharlieb cannot! Is it not ridiculous?
records.t:
women doctors are excluded from medical societies (despite their qualifications and hospital work), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
And that man, you know, can be a fellow of the colleges, and member of any society he likes to apply to, while Mrs. G. Anderson and Mrs. Scharlieb cannot! Is it not ridiculous?

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: medical education requires mixed school (in Elsie Inglis’s view for Edinburgh)
records.q: You know you must not aim at a separate but at a mixed school in Edinburgh. I am sure this is best, and all the women here think so too.
records.t:
medical education requires mixed school (in Elsie Inglis’s view for Edinburgh), 1918, Dr. Elsie Inglis
You know you must not aim at a separate but at a mixed school in Edinburgh. I am sure this is best, and all the women here think so too.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ PREFACE The story of Elsie Inglis needs little introduction.
records.s: The preface introduces Elsie Inglis as a courageous and principled woman who consistently followed her convictions and used every opportunity to serve others. It describes her as honest, affectionate, devoted to liberty, and representative of the spirit of her nation and race. The memoir is based on accounts from her family, friends, patients, and Units, and aims to present a faithful portrait of her. It also asks readers not to forget the patients in the Hospice and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, which are described as her living memorials.

She is remembered as one of old Scotia’s truest daughters, and the preface says that she continues to speak through her example and works.

records.s: This unit traces the Inglis family from Kingsmills, Inverness-shire, through Alexander Inglis’s emigration to Carolina, David Inglis’s career in India, and John Inglis’s distinguished service in the Indian colonial administration. Alexander Inglis’s loyalty to the British Government led to the confiscation of his Charleston estates, and he later died from wounds received in a duel. David Inglis served the East India Company in India, while John Inglis became a senior administrator in the Punjab, Rohilcund, Oude, and the North-West Provinces. The unit also describes Harriet Louis Thompson’s family life and religious work, the faithful Indian nurse Sona, the Indian Mutiny, and the family’s recurring combination of Scottish heritage, activity, travel, and religious faith.

records.s: Alexander Inglis, Elsie Inglis’s great-grandfather, married Mary Deas and emigrated to Carolina around 1780, leaving his four children to be educated in Scotland. He became a Charleston merchant and property owner, remained loyal to the British Government during the American conflict, and died from wounds received in a duel in 1791.

records.s: David Inglis, Alexander’s son and Elsie Inglis’s grandfather, was raised in Scotland by his uncle William Inglis and joined the East India Company as a writer in 1798. He served during the Mahratta War, administered territorial cessions of the Peshwa under the Treaty of Bassein, later entered business in Bombay, married Martha Money in 1806, and returned to England in 1812.

records.s: John Inglis, born in 1820, studied at Haileybury and entered the Indian Civil Service after learning the language in Calcutta. He served at Agra and in the Punjab, took part in the suppression of the Indian Mutiny, became Commissioner of Rohilcund, served on the Board of Revenue, joined the Legislative Council of India, and was Chief Commissioner of Oude from 1875 to 1877.

records.s: The Punjab was the province to which John Inglis was transferred in 1847 and where he served at Sealkote. He later returned during the Indian Mutiny and worked in the region during its settlement, gaining the confidence and affection of Sikhs, Punjabis, and Rajpoots.

records.s: Harriet Louis Thompson, John Inglis’s wife, was the daughter of an early Indian civilian and one of nine sisters who mostly married into the Indian Civil Service. She was an accomplished rider and driver, deeply religious, and while living in Southampton during a separation from her husband, she founded and ran a large working-men’s club where she gave Sunday religious lectures.

records.s: Sona was an Indian ayah who served the Inglis family for more than thirty years and accompanied some of them to England during the 1857 crisis. She became a Christian, was baptized in 1877, and was later regarded as one of the pillars of the Indian Christian Church in Lucknow.

records.s: The outbreak of the Indian Mutiny in 1857 caused John Inglis to return to India while Harriet Louis Thompson remained in England with six children and their ayah. John Inglis served in the suppression of the Mutiny, including the action at Najibabad, the recapture of Bareilly, and the pacification of Rohilcund.

records.s: The British Empire in India provided the setting for the Inglis family’s official careers and separations. John Inglis served in its civil administration and military operations, while the family’s experience included travel between India and Britain and close relationships with Indian subjects and servants.

records.s: The Indian colonial administration employed John Inglis in increasingly senior roles, including assistant magistrate, magistrate, Commissioner of Rohilcund, member of the Board of Revenue, member of the Legislative Council of India, and Chief Commissioner of Oude. His work involved civil government, territorial transfers, the suppression of rebellion, and the post-Mutiny settlement of provinces.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: This unit describes Elsie Maud Inglis’s birth and childhood in India, including her early travels, vivid personality, intelligence, and strong will. It portrays her close companionship with her father, Mr. Inglis, and the religious and family life fostered by both parents. Her sisters’ memories and family letters record her imaginative play, independent character, education, and early interest in the world around her. The unit presents Mr. Inglis’s commitment to giving his daughters equal opportunities and links Elsie’s upbringing to her later service to mankind.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: Elsie Maud Inglis was born at Naini Tal in August 1864 and was described as a healthy, observant, intelligent, cheerful, and strong-willed child. She travelled extensively with her parents, formed a particularly close companionship with her father, enjoyed stories and imaginative games, and showed early independence and perseverance.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: Mr. Inglis was a devoted and affectionate father who shared walks, breakfasts, correspondence, and religious life with his daughters. He was especially close to Elsie, treated the three sisters equally, supported their mother’s authority, and sought equal opportunities and the best education for his daughters.

records.l: Mrs. Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: Mrs. Inglis cared for Elsie and her sisters, recorded their early development, taught them prayers and Bible lessons, and guided their daily life. She is remembered as a quiet, strong mother whose eyes and smile remained influential in her children’s memories.

records.l: Naini Tal, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: Naini Tal was the place where Elsie was born and where the family spent part of each year. It was a beautiful Himalayan hill station with views of distant snow-crowned ranges, and it provided the setting for the family’s walks, breakfasts, and childhood memories.

records.l: India, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: India was the setting of Elsie’s early childhood, divided between the hot plains and the hills. The family travelled through India by palki and spent time at places including Naini Tal, while Elsie became accustomed to long journeys and varied surroundings.

records.l: Elsie's birth, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: Elsie’s birth took place at Naini Tal on August 16, 1864. Her mother and the new baby were reported to be well, and the family welcomed her as a strong and healthy child.

records.l: the Inglis family's childhood, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: The Inglis family’s childhood was marked by affection, religious practice, outdoor life, travel, and close companionship among the three sisters and their parents. The children shared walks, lessons, imaginative games with dolls, and memories of an equal and loving father.

records.l: Elsie's education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: Elsie was taught by a governess, Mrs. Marwood, and found learning easy. She enjoyed stories, received Bible lessons and prayers from her mother, and was intended by her father to receive the best and highest education.

records.l: women's intellectual freedom, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: The unit places Elsie’s birth in the early movement that held that women could possess minds and brains of their own and should be free to cultivate them. It contrasts this outlook with the instruction given to many women that their lives should be devoted to male relatives without independent education or provision.

records.l: service to mankind, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER II ELSIE MAUD INGLIS 1864-1917 ‘Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is His reward.
records.s: The unit presents Elsie’s later career as a life of womanly grace and sustaining service. It suggests that she first learned the secret of service to mankind through the loving, equal, and purposeful home created by her father.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: This unit describes the Inglis family’s move from India to Tasmania, Edinburgh, and Paris between 1876 and 1885, focusing especially on Elsie Inglis’s education and developing character. Mr. Inglis retired from service after serving as Chief Commissioner of Oude and later supported Elsie through correspondence and intellectual companionship. Elsie attended school in Tasmania and at the Charlotte Square Institution, where she showed initiative, edited the school magazine, and secured permission for girls to play in Charlotte Square gardens. After returning from Paris in 1883, Elsie’s mother died of scarlet fever, and Elsie assumed responsibility for her father and household, recording resolutions for her conduct.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Mr. Inglis retired after serving as Chief Commissioner of Oude, having received high praise from Lord Lytton. He moved with his family to Tasmania and then Edinburgh, corresponded closely with Elsie during her Paris education, and shared a deep intellectual and affectionate fellowship with her. After Mrs. Inglis’s death, he relied on Elsie, who took on his burdens and remained his support until his death.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Elsie attended school in Tasmania, the Charlotte Square Institution in Edinburgh, and later a school in Paris. She showed initiative by securing permission for girls to play in Charlotte Square gardens, edited the Edina, and was remembered for her confidence, intellect, compassion, and strong character. After her mother’s death, she became the main support of her father and resolved to be more truthful, thorough, and responsible.

records.l: Mrs. Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Mrs. Inglis moved with her family from India to Tasmania and Edinburgh and corresponded with Elsie during her time in Paris. She helped decide that Elsie should go to Paris and joined Mr. Inglis in praying for guidance about the decision. After Elsie returned, Mrs. Inglis died from a virulent attack of scarlet fever.

records.l: Elsie Inglis’s family and kindred, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: The Inglis family left India after Mr. Inglis retired, spent two years in Hobart settling two sons on the land, and then made Edinburgh their home. The family lived at 70 Bruntsfield Place, sent Elsie and Eva to school, and supported Elsie’s education in Paris.

records.l: Charlotte Square Institution, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: The Charlotte Square Institution was the Edinburgh school for girls, where Elsie and her sister Eva attended under Mr. Oliphant. Elsie distinguished herself academically, edited the Edina, and persuaded the directors and neighbouring proprietors to allow the girls to play in Charlotte Square gardens.

records.l: India, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: India was the place of Mr. Inglis’s long public service, including his work as Chief Commissioner of Oude. The Inglis family left India after his retirement, and Mr. Inglis later recalled to Elsie an incident from her childhood there when she went for a walk and was thought to be lost.

records.l: Tasmania, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Tasmania was where two of Mr. Inglis’s sons had settled and where the family spent two years before returning to Britain. Elsie and Eva attended a good school there, and Elsie helped establish school colours with Miss Knott’s support.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Edinburgh became the Inglis family’s home after their time in Tasmania, and Elsie and Eva attended the Charlotte Square Institution there. Elsie formed lasting friendships and intellectual associations in Edinburgh, including the Six Sincere Students Society.

records.l: Paris, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Paris was where Elsie went to school in September 1882 with Miss Brown and six other girls. During her stay, she corresponded with her parents about life and events, although her parents found that the experience did not give her a French accent or strong musical abilities.

records.l: the Paris education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: The Paris education ended in the summer of 1883. Miss Brown remembered the sadness of the girls’ departure and encouraged them to continue reading French aloud, while Elsie’s family regarded her French and music as less successful than hoped.

records.l: scarlet fever, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Scarlet fever caused Mrs. Inglis’s death shortly after Elsie returned from Paris. Its loss left Mr. Inglis without the central support of his loving nature and led Elsie to assume responsibility for him and the household.

records.l: Elsie’s resolutions, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER III THE LADDER OF LEARNING 1876-1885 ‘Hast thou come with the heart of thy childhood back: The free, the pure, the kind?
records.s: Elsie’s resolutions were written in pencil after her mother’s death, when she became the support of her father. She resolved to stop dreaming and making stories, control her temper, devote more attention to housekeeping, become more thorough and truthful, and seek God’s help.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: This unit describes Elsie Inglis’s student years from 1885 to 1892, when she began medical study at the Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women and continued her studies from her father’s home. It explains the barriers facing women in higher and medical education, including restricted clinical teaching, extra fees, poor instruction, and exclusion from mixed classes. Elsie Inglis strongly opposed what she considered unjust treatment of students, including Dr. Jex Blake’s expulsion of two students, while remaining influenced by her father’s commitment to equal justice. The unit also records aspects of her student life, including her religious observance, long walks with Mr. Inglis, strong sense of fair play, and encouragement of women studying medicine.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Elsie Inglis recognised her vocation to study medicine and began her first medical teaching at the Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women. She opposed what she regarded as unjust treatment, including the expulsion of two students by Dr. Jex Blake, and secretly marked the examination list to refute claims that Student Christian Union members neglected their studies. During her student years she studied from her father’s home, worshipped with him, walked extensively, and developed a strong commitment to fair play and women’s causes.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Mr. Inglis responded calmly and practically when Elsie Inglis announced her intention to study medicine, working to overcome the obstacles in her way. After Mrs. Inglis’s death, he moved with the family to rooms in Melville Street, where Elsie continued her studies from his home. He was a high-minded and chivalrous influence on Elsie, and she took long walks with him after her mother died.

records.l: Dr. Jex Blake, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Dr. Jex Blake founded the Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women, where Elsie Inglis received her first medical teaching. She expelled two students for failing to observe the school’s discipline, but a lawsuit established that their treatment had been unjustified. Elsie Inglis continued to acknowledge Dr. Jex Blake’s important pioneering work despite their profound disagreement over the school’s management.

records.l: University Commissioners, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: The University Commission decided that women should no longer be excluded from university degrees because of their sex. Its decision followed questions about the justice and benefit of excluding women, and it enabled the Scottish Universities to open their degrees to all students.

records.l: Scottish Universities, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: The Scottish Universities opened their degrees to all students after the University Commission determined that women should not be excluded because of their sex.

records.l: Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: The Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women was founded by Dr. Jex Blake and provided Elsie Inglis with her first medical teaching. Its students faced the wider difficulties imposed on women seeking medical education, including restricted clinical opportunities and opposition from parts of the profession.

records.l: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh refused to admit women to clinical teaching in its wards until they raised seven hundred pounds to furnish two wards for their use. Women remained confined mainly to those two wards, with only limited access to other subjects.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Edinburgh was the setting for Elsie Inglis’s early medical studies and for the institutional barriers confronting women students. Elsie later became known as a good physician in her native city and in allied nations.

records.l: women’s higher education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Women’s higher education was still in its early stages, and each advance had to be fought for against obscurantism and professional jealousy. Although university commissions issued reports supporting access, their implementation was left to people who often sought to exclude women from the medical profession.

records.l: medical education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Women’s medical education was hindered by the refusal of mixed classes, limited hospital teaching, difficult arrangements for extra-mural instruction, additional fees, and inadequate teaching by some professors. Women students nevertheless raised the funds demanded by the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh to obtain clinical instruction.

records.l: women’s admission to the medical profession, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Women’s admission to the medical profession required them to overcome opposition, professional jealousy, restricted clinical access, and financial barriers. Women had staunch supporters among doctors, but the profession as a whole was described as insufficiently willing to share its knowledge with them.

records.l: University degrees for women, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: The University Commission decided that women could no longer be excluded from university degrees on account of their sex. The Scottish Universities subsequently opened their degrees to all students.

records.l: Elsie Inglis’s student years, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER IV THE STUDENT DAYS 1885-1892 EDINBURGH--GLASGOW ‘Let knowledge grow from more to more, But more of reverence in us dwell; That mind and soul, according well, May make one music as before, But vaster.
records.s: Elsie Inglis’s student years from 1885 to 1892 were spent amid difficult and changing conditions for women studying medicine. She lived and studied with Mr. Inglis, attended worship with him, took long walks, and became known for her sense of justice, encouragement of women medical students, and interest in women’s causes.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis went to Glasgow in 1891 to study for the Triple Qualification, because she could not take surgery in Edinburgh and Glasgow offered better clinical teaching. At the Medical School in Glasgow, she trained in hospital wards and dispensaries under doctors including Dr. MacEwan while living at the Y.W.C.A. Hostel. She and the other women students fought the Glasgow Infirmary Managers’ attempt to exclude them from mixed classes and eventually secured access to the classes. Elsie passed her examination with great success and continued toward a career in medicine.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis went to Glasgow in 1891 to take the examination for the Triple Qualification and to obtain clinical experience unavailable to her in Edinburgh. She studied intensively, attended hospital wards and dispensaries, took part in the campaign for women’s access to mixed classes, and passed the examination with great success.

records.l: Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Glasgow offered Elsie Inglis more favourable facilities for clinical teaching than Edinburgh. Its hospital and medical school became the setting for her training, examination preparation, and participation in the fight over mixed classes.

records.l: Triple Qualification, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Triple Qualification was the examination Elsie Inglis went to Glasgow to take in 1891. She passed it with great success after her period of study and clinical training.

records.l: Medical School in Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Medical School in Glasgow provided Elsie Inglis with clinical teaching and access to hospital wards and dispensaries. Women students there faced opposition over their attendance at mixed classes.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis could not then take surgery in Edinburgh, making Glasgow a more suitable place for her clinical training. Edinburgh was also the site of competing efforts to establish medical education for women.

records.l: Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women was founded by Dr. Jex Blake. It was distinct from the Medical College for Women promoted by Elsie Inglis and other women students.

records.l: Medical College for Women, Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Medical College for Women was promoted by Elsie Inglis and other women students in Edinburgh. Elsie was more closely associated with its fortunes than with those of the Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women.

records.l: Dr. MacEwan, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Dr. MacEwan taught and supervised Elsie Inglis in the wards, questioned her closely, allowed her to assist with an operation, and encouraged her surgical training. He supported the women students during the dispute over mixed classes and believed women should ultimately attend the same schools as men.

records.l: Sir William MacEwan, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Sir William MacEwan is identified as the later name of Dr. MacEwan. The text credits him with enjoying the fight over women students’ access to classes and suggests that the success of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals reflected, in part, the influence of his teaching.

records.l: Royal Infirmary of Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Royal Infirmary of Glasgow is described as nearly as large and quite as rich as the Edinburgh Royal. It had a large hospital, but the text criticizes the lack of comparable teaching arrangements.

records.l: St Andrews, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: St Andrews had opened degrees and mixed classes, with further mixed classes planned from the following October. Its developments were cited as evidence of changing attitudes toward women’s university education.

records.l: the University of Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Glasgow University was expected to grant degrees in Arts, Medicine, Science, and Theology from October after Queen Margaret College became an integral part of the University. The changes were presented as placing women’s education on the same footing as men’s.

records.l: Glasgow Infirmary Managers, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Glasgow Infirmary Managers repeatedly opposed women students attending mixed classes, including after the students had paid fees for the full medical course. Their decision led to organized resistance and was eventually abandoned.

records.l: Dr. T., Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Dr. T. conveyed the Glasgow Infirmary Managers’ decision that women students were not to attend mixed classes. After resistance from the students and their supporters, he eventually conveyed that they could attend any of the classes.

records.l: Queen Margaret’s College, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Queen Margaret College was to become an integral part of the University rather than merely being affiliated with it. Its lecturers were to be appointed again by the Senators, supporting the granting of Glasgow degrees in several subjects.

records.l: Medical College for Women campaign, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The Medical College for Women campaign sought to promote a women’s medical college in Edinburgh. Elsie Inglis referred to wanting money for a woman’s college there, although she also agreed that women should attend the same schools as men if they were admitted.

records.l: women students' campaign for mixed classes, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The women students’ campaign for mixed classes challenged the Glasgow Infirmary Managers’ attempt to exclude women from shared teaching. The students used their fees, legal grievances, and support from sympathetic medical leaders to secure access.

records.l: medical education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Women’s medical education was expanding through new colleges, degrees, and mixed classes. The text presents the movement as part of a broader change toward placing women’s education on the same footing as men’s.

records.l: mixed classes, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Mixed classes were classes attended by both women and men. The Glasgow Infirmary Managers opposed women students’ attendance, but the women eventually won the right to attend any of the classes.

records.l: medical training, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis received medical training through hospital wards, dispensaries, operations, clinical observation, and examination preparation in Glasgow. Her training included surgery and was supported by teachers such as Dr. MacEwan.

records.l: surgery, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis could not take surgery in Edinburgh at the time, so she studied it in Glasgow. Dr. MacEwan allowed her to assist with an operation, and she worked to prepare herself for the surgical part of her qualification.

records.l: medical examination, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis prepared for the medical examination while studying and working in Glasgow. Despite worries about her memory and the questions she might face, she passed the examination with great success.

records.l: women's professional equality, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: The unit presents women’s professional equality as a goal advanced through access to medical schools, mixed classes, university degrees, and professional training. The women students’ successful resistance to exclusion is described as part of a wider struggle for democratic rights in education.

records.l: Medical College for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ In 1891 Elsie went to Glasgow to take the examination for the Triple Qualifica
records.s: Elsie Inglis said that she wanted the first £20,000 she encountered to build and endow a woman’s college in Edinburgh. She regarded such a college as a possible response to the refusal to admit women to existing institutions.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: After completing her clinical work and passing the Triple Qualification in Glasgow in 1892, Elsie Inglis became house-surgeon at the New Hospital for Women in London. She described the hospital’s wards, staff, patients, operations, outpatient department, and daily demands in detailed letters to her father. Elsie worked with Garrett Anderson, Mrs. Scharlieb, and other women doctors, while observing the difficulties and opportunities facing women in medical practice and education. She hoped eventually to establish a hospital in Edinburgh and supported a mixed medical school there.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Elsie Inglis completed her clinical work in Glasgow, passed the Triple Qualification in 1892, and became house-surgeon at the New Hospital for Women in London. She worked energetically, managed wards and students, assisted with operations, wrote daily letters to her father, and hoped to establish a hospital in Edinburgh.

records.l: Garrett Anderson, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Garrett Anderson worked at the New Hospital for Women and was described by Elsie as an active and influential doctor. She advised Elsie about maternity work, took her to a hospital dance, invited her to assist with a small operation, and encouraged her professional development.

records.l: Mrs. Scharlieb, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Mrs. Scharlieb was a visiting doctor at the New Hospital for Women and worked with Elsie on ward care and operations. She was particular but kind, discussed the hospital’s future as a qualifying institution, advised Elsie about her work, and expected eventually to be consulted when Elsie became a surgeon.

records.l: New Hospital for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: The New Hospital for Women in Euston Road had been established for nearly thirty years when Elsie joined it. It had four main wards, two smaller wards for serious cases, an extensive outpatient department, and a staff and student body largely organized around women doctors.

records.l: London, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: London was where Elsie worked at the New Hospital for Women from 1892 to 1893. During her residence she visited churches, attended sermons, went to theatres and dances, and assisted Garrett Anderson with an operation.

records.l: Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Glasgow was where Elsie completed her clinical work before passing the Triple Qualification in 1892. She compared its practice with London hospitals, particularly regarding students’ administration of anaesthetics.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Elsie hoped to establish a hospital of her own in Edinburgh. She argued that Edinburgh should aim for a mixed medical school rather than a separate school for women, while considering how women students might be accommodated if sent to Leith.

records.l: women doctors, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Women doctors at the New Hospital for Women had achieved substantial work despite exclusion and discouragement, but some, including Garrett Anderson and Mrs. Scharlieb, were barred from fellowship of the colleges and membership of certain societies. The hospital’s success, including more than 20,000 outpatient visits in the year up to November, was presented as evidence that women doctors were wanted.

records.l: patients, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Patients at the hospital included women whose illnesses had previously been dismissed as hysteria and others who had been given alarming or mistaken diagnoses. Elsie observed that patients with courage and stable nerves often recovered more quickly, and she described the hospital’s efforts to provide treatment, sunshine, and careful postoperative care.

records.l: medical education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Students from the School of Medicine served as dressers and clerks at the New Hospital for Women, although their principal hospital was the Royal Free. The hospital’s doctors discussed making it a qualifying hospital, which would require men’s beds and a mixed staff, while Elsie advocated a mixed school in Edinburgh.

records.l: medical practice, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: The unit shows medical practice involving ward rounds, high-temperature monitoring, galvanic cautery, anaesthesia, operations, outpatient care, and consultation. It also records disputes over diagnoses, the treatment of illnesses labeled hysteria, and differing Scottish and London approaches to observing patients under anaesthesia.

records.l: operations, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: Operations were a regular part of life at the New Hospital for Women, and Elsie assisted with several major cases. Some proceeded successfully, while one patient died after apparently doing well because she lacked the vitality to withstand the shock.

records.l: women’s hospital movement, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER V LONDON THE NEW HOSPITAL FOR WOMEN DUBLIN THE ROTUNDA 1892-1894 ‘We take up the task eternal and the burden and the lesson, Pioneers, O Pioneers.
records.s: The New Hospital for Women represented the principle that women could practise the healing art and formed part of the wider women’s hospital movement. Its history was associated with Elizabeth Blackwell, Sophia Jex Blake, Garrett Anderson, and the growing professional work of women doctors.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Elsie Inglis undertakes a three-month midwifery course at the Rotunda in Dublin, where she gains extensive practical experience but finds that women are not given the same opportunities as men. She considers continuing her training in Paris and beginning a medical practice in Edinburgh with Miss MacGregor, potentially including a dispensary and hospital for female students. During her stay she discusses Irish politics, women’s suffrage, medical work, and the difficulties faced by women doctors. She returns home shortly before her father, John Inglis, dies on March 13, 1894, leaving her deeply bereaved.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Elsie Inglis takes a three-month midwifery course at the Rotunda in Dublin and works extensively with patients and childbirth cases. She observes that women students are not deliberately excluded but are routinely overlooked when senior clinical work is assigned to men. She plans to return to Edinburgh, possibly to work with Miss MacGregor, but her father’s death shortly after her return leaves her feeling that life and work have lost their purpose.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: John Inglis is Elsie’s father, to whom she writes about her training, health, work, and plans for an Edinburgh practice. He becomes seriously ill while she is in Dublin, and she returns to receive his welcome. He dies after suffering borne with quiet patience, remembered by his old Indian friends as upright, straightforward, and highly principled.

records.l: the Rotunda, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: The Rotunda in Dublin provides Elsie with three months of clinical training in midwifery. She praises its methods and the experience it gives her, but notes that male senior students receive opportunities to undertake much of the clinical work that women students are not offered.

records.l: Dublin, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Dublin is where Elsie stays at Costigan’s Hotel while training at the Rotunda from November 1893 into February 1894. During her stay she attends patients, encounters Irish political and religious divisions, and considers further study in Paris before returning to Edinburgh.

records.l: women’s suffrage, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Elsie follows political developments concerning women’s suffrage and celebrates the franchise being carried for parish councils. She argues about suffrage with Dr. B., who later tells her that she was right and becomes a convert to the cause.

records.l: Dr. Jessie MacGregor, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Miss MacGregor writes to Elsie about starting medical work together in Edinburgh. Elsie regards her as a splendid pathologist and one of the best women doctors, and thinks their combined work could benefit both of them.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Edinburgh is the place where Elsie expects to begin her medical career after returning from Dublin. She considers establishing a practice there with Miss MacGregor, living at home while using consulting rooms elsewhere.

records.l: midwifery, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Elsie’s training in midwifery at the Rotunda gives her confidence and extensive practical experience in the field. She feels that the Rotunda’s methods have prepared her to do important work in this branch of medicine.

records.l: the three-month Rotunda course, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: The three-month Rotunda course teaches Elsie a great deal about midwifery and makes her feel established in the subject. After three months she is told that she has learned all the Rotunda can teach her; she considers spending another three months studying in Paris instead of remaining for the six-month examination and Licentiate of Midwifery.

records.l: women doctors, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: The unit shows that women doctors face assumptions that women cannot be doctors and are often overlooked for clinical opportunities given to men. Elsie also describes capable women doctors, including Miss D., who holds an M.B. and receives a travelling bursary, and Miss MacGregor, whom she considers a leading woman pathologist.

records.l: the proposed Edinburgh practice, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: Elsie considers starting a medical practice in Edinburgh with Miss MacGregor. They discuss working together, establishing a dispensary, and eventually creating a hospital like the Rotunda where female students could live on the premises.

records.l: John Inglis’s death, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ The next course Elsie decided on taking was one of three months in Midwifery i
records.s: John Inglis dies on March 13, 1894, shortly after Elsie returns from Dublin. Elsie describes his quiet patience and says that she cannot imagine life without him, especially because they had made plans for her medical work that he had hoped to see begin.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: This unit describes Elsie Inglis’s political and public life, especially her support for women’s suffrage, Liberal politics, and Home Rule. It presents John Inglis’s progressive view of equality and mutual respect within marriage and his influence on Elsie’s independent thought. Elsie connects the vote to women’s ability to challenge abusive husbands and improve laws affecting women’s health and welfare. The unit also records her views on the Home Rule question, Ireland, the Labour movement, and the Representation of the People’s Bill, which marked the achievement of political enfranchisement.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: Elsie Inglis supported women’s suffrage and Liberal politics and was a convinced Home Ruler. Through her medical work, she saw how husbands and laws could deny women necessary treatment, strengthening her belief that women needed the vote. She wrote and spoke about women’s rights, Home Rule, labour questions, and related political issues.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: John Inglis expressed an advanced view of marriage, urging husbands to respect their wives as equal companions, confidential friends, and mutual sources of comfort. His outlook appears to have influenced Elsie Inglis’s sympathetic independence and freedom of thought.

records.l: Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: Glasgow was where Elsie Inglis studied and practised medicine, attended political and medical meetings, and wrote to her father about women’s rights, Home Rule, labour questions, and local political discussion.

records.l: Ireland, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: Ireland was the subject of the Home Rule controversy discussed by Elsie Inglis and her father. Elsie supported giving Ireland control over its own affairs while preserving the unity of the Empire, and she argued that Irish members should remain in Parliament.

records.l: the Representation of the People’s Bill, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: The Representation of the People’s Bill is presented as the measure that marked the victory of the common cause for which Elsie Inglis and her comrades had worked: women’s political enfranchisement.

records.l: the Home Rule Bill of 1893, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: Elsie Inglis regarded the groundwork of the Home Rule Bill of 1893 as sound, though she believed it could be improved in committee. She supported retaining Irish members in Parliament and considered the proposed transfer of powers over police and land workable over time.

records.l: the Home Rule question, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: The Home Rule question occupied Elsie Inglis’s political attention during the 1890s. She supported Home Rule, criticised obstruction and Lord Salisbury’s encouragement of resistance, and considered possible arrangements combining Irish self-government with Imperial Federation.

records.l: women’s suffrage, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: Elsie Inglis treated women’s suffrage as a genuinely Liberal issue and criticised political parties and women’s organisations for placing party interests before it. She believed the vote would help women resist domestic oppression and expose abuses such as husbands preventing wives from receiving medical treatment.

records.l: political enfranchisement, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER VI POLITICAL ENFRANCHISEMENT AND NATIONAL POLITICS ‘Well done, New Zealand!
records.s: Political enfranchisement is presented as the common cause achieved at the end of the period described. The unit links its achievement to the Representation of the People’s Bill and to the long campaign against women’s exclusion on the basis of sex.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: This unit portrays Dr. Elsie Inglis as a pioneering doctor, organiser, and leader in the women’s suffrage movement. It describes her work for women as sanitary inspectors, her organisational leadership in the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, and her opposition to militant suffragism. Her suffrage colleagues depict her as fair-minded, encouraging, disciplined, and devoted to extending women’s citizenship. The unit also connects the organised support of Scottish suffrage societies with the later creation of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals and Inglis’s wartime service.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Dr. Elsie Inglis was an early woman doctor to speak at a Sanitary Congress, where she advocated employing women as sanitary inspectors. She became a leading organiser in the women’s suffrage movement, serving as Honorary Secretary of the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, opposing militant suffragism, and giving her time and resources to the cause. Her colleagues remembered her as courageous, fair-minded, encouraging, disciplined, and devoted to helping the weak.

records.l: Scotland, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Scotland was the setting for much of Dr. Elsie Inglis’s suffrage organising, including her work in the Highlands and with the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies. Scottish women’s organised support later helped Inglis establish units and equipment for wartime medical work.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Serbia is mentioned as a place where Dr. Elsie Inglis later continued her demanding work. Her characteristic habit of writing despite difficult travel conditions is said to have continued there.

records.l: the British Parliament, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Parliament had long treated women’s franchise as an academic or marginal issue, with private members’ Bills often being talked out or talked round. After 1906, the question became a major unresolved political issue that placed pressure on successive Governments.

records.l: women’s suffrage, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: The women’s suffrage movement expanded rapidly after 1906, multiplying meetings, raising funds, organising debates, and coordinating societies. Dr. Elsie Inglis was a prominent organiser within its constitutional and law-abiding wing.

records.l: political enfranchisement, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Women’s franchise changed from being widely regarded as a crank cause to becoming a major democratic and political issue after the 1906 elections. The movement sought free rights of citizenship for women through organised pressure on Parliament.

records.l: militant suffragism, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Militant suffragism emerged alongside the strengthened suffrage campaign and gave the press extensive publicity. Dr. Elsie Inglis deplored its law-breaking and believed that claiming a right to do wrong for a good purpose was closely related to anarchy.

records.l: Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: The Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies was carefully organised and coordinated to bring pressure to bear on Parliament. Dr. Elsie Inglis served as its Honorary Secretary and strongly influenced its policy between 1906 and 1914.

records.l: Suffrage societies, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Scottish suffrage societies provided organisation and workers for the establishment of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. They supported Dr. Elsie Inglis’s work and its ideals even when the wider community wished to separate the hospitals from the unpopular suffrage cause.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals were started with the organisation and workers supplied by Scottish suffrage societies. Their work later became widely praised, although speakers were sometimes asked to avoid mentioning the suffrage cause that had helped make them possible.

records.l: women as citizens or as doctors, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Women are presented as seeking full citizenship, participation in public administration, and a greater role in the Church and State. The unit argues that women’s organised work had already made substantial contributions, despite continuing institutional prejudice against them.

records.l: the Vote, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: The Vote was the central political objective repeatedly invoked by Dr. Elsie Inglis and her colleagues. She greeted supporters with hopes for a good year and the Vote, and described it as the weapon women could use to help build the New Jerusalem.

records.l: the Suffrage movement’s organisation, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: The Suffrage movement’s organisation expanded through federated societies, coordinated workers, fundraising, meetings, debates, and a press campaign. Dr. Elsie Inglis’s administrative ability and ability to seize opportunities were described as important to this development.

records.l: the First World War, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: The First World War is not named directly, but the unit refers to Dr. Elsie Inglis going to the battle fronts of the world and aiding nations allied in arms. Her wartime work is presented as an achievement made possible by the strength and support of Scottish suffrage women.

records.l: women’s medical service in wartime, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ Another friend writes:-- ‘I should like to send you a recollection of her in t
records.s: Women’s medical service in wartime is represented through the units and equipment that Dr. Elsie Inglis brought into existence for the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. These services earned praise from allied nations and grew out of the organisation and support of Scottish suffrage societies.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: This unit describes Dr. Elsie Inglis’s medical practice, political work, and development of institutions serving women, mothers, infants, students, and poor local families in Edinburgh. She graduated M.B., C.M. from the University of Edinburgh in 1899, studied surgical and clinical methods abroad, and later acquired substantial surgical skill through the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. She campaigned for women’s medical education and enfranchisement, helped establish the Muir Hall of Residence, and founded the Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh as a maternity and infant-welfare centre staffed by medical women. The unit also records her extensive personal care for patients and local families, whom she treated with practical authority, generosity, and affection.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Dr. Elsie Inglis practised medicine in Edinburgh, worked in partnership with Dr. Jessie MacGregor, and graduated M.B., C.M. in 1899. She combined medical practice with political and suffrage work, founded and directed institutions for women and families, studied medicine abroad, and cared personally for poor patients and local households. She was described as indomitable, generous, practical, and deeply committed to improving women’s opportunities and public welfare.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Elsie Inglis’s father was the centre and mainspring of her existence, and he had been glad to see her begin her professional career. After his death, she said that she could not imagine life without him, but she continued her work and became a source of support to many members of his extended household.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals gave Dr. Inglis the opportunity to acquire considerable surgical skill under intense wartime pressure. Her work there included long periods at the operating table and demonstrated what a great surgeon she might have become with equal opportunities during her peace practice.

records.l: University of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: The University of Edinburgh admitted women to its medical degree examinations, and Dr. Inglis graduated M.B., C.M. there in 1899. The University had previously refused to admit women medical students or recognise certain extra-mural mixed classes, but in 1916, under a new head, it opened its doors to women medical students.

records.l: Scottish medical profession, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: The medical profession restricted women through limited clinical opportunities, inadequate laboratory access, and opposition to their full participation in medical education. Dr. Inglis fought these restrictions and sought equal opportunities for men and women in study, laboratory work, and professional practice.

records.l: medical education, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Women’s medical education was affected by separate lectures that Dr. Inglis considered inferior to those offered to men and by women students’ lack of thorough laboratory practice before examinations. She challenged the University authorities, lectured on gynecology at a medical college for women, and supported institutions that gave women students better opportunities.

records.l: women’s suffrage, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Women’s suffrage was one of Dr. Inglis’s principal political commitments. She devoted substantial time to the campaign for women’s political enfranchisement and eventually left party organisation when she believed that working independently would better advance the cause.

records.l: Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: The Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh opened in 1904 as a maternity home in a poorer district, with an operating theatre and eight beds. It later became devoted to maternity and infant-welfare cases, trained nurses for the C.M.B. examination, and developed facilities including a baby clinic, milk depot, health centres, and a ward for malnutrition cases.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Edinburgh was the centre of Dr. Inglis’s medical, political, educational, and philanthropic work. She practised there, founded the Hospice in the High Street, supported women students, worked with local organisations, and cared for families living between Morrison Street and the High Street.

records.l: Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Dr. Inglis joined the Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association in its early organised years and served as its Vice-President for sixteen years. She was one of its most active members, valued as a speaker and adviser, and respected for her enthusiasm for women’s welfare and her clear political judgment.

records.l: the Liberal Party, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Dr. Inglis was connected with the Liberal Party through the Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association and the Women’s Liberal League. She severed her connection with the party when she became convinced that she could advance the cause of women more effectively without attachment to a party organisation.

records.l: Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: The Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students was founded in George Square to provide suitable accommodation for women students coming to the University from the country. Dr. Inglis served as honorary secretary until her death, helped students with illness and personal difficulties, and worked for their comfort.

records.l: Maternity Hospice nursing and infant-welfare work, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: The Maternity Hospice nursing and infant-welfare work grew from a nursing home for working women into a maternity and infant-welfare centre serving a poorer district. Dr. Inglis promoted home visits, nurse training, infant care, a milk depot, health centres, and care designed around patients’ comfort and local needs.

records.l: women doctors, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ CHAPTER VII THE PROFESSION AND THE FAITH ‘Run the straight race through God’s good grace, Lift up thine eyes and seek His face; Life with its way before us lies, Christ is the path, and Christ the prize.
records.s: Medical women staffed the Hospice and received professional opportunities there that were denied to them in other maternity hospitals. Dr. Inglis supported their education, clinical work, and access to laboratories and professional recognition.

records.s: This unit concerns Dr. Elsie Inglis’s medical work, family life, spiritual development, recreation, and disciplined daily habits. She treated rich and poor alike, combining trained skill with sympathy, and drew increasing strength from her faith. Her sisters, nieces, friends, and household formed an important part of her life, while holidays, family prayers, and social gatherings gave her rest and companionship. After her father’s death, she found a settled spiritual home in the Church of Scotland through the ministry and friendship of Dr. Wallace Williamson, and she faced the coming international crisis with steadfastness.

records.s: This unit describes how the outbreak of World War I transformed opportunities for women and enabled Elsie Maud Inglis to establish the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. The War Office rejected her offer of medical service, but French and Serbian authorities later welcomed the hospitals. Inglis mobilised women from the Women’s Suffrage movement, formed a committee through the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies and the Scottish Federation, and sought funds for hospital units serving the Allied nations. By October 1914, the Scottish Women’s Hospitals scheme had been adopted and was being organised for service with the Serbian army.
