records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: This unit describes the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ work in Serbia and Russia during the war, including their efforts against typhus, typhoid, famine fevers, and other suffering. Dr. Elsie Inglis directed the hospitals’ organization and later took personal charge of the unit in Serbia, while Dr. Eleanor Soltau led the First Serbian Unit until illness forced her to stop. The Foreign Office and Admiralty supported the hospitals’ equipment, transport, and safety, despite the dangers faced by the women. Serbia commemorated Dr. Inglis and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals with a fountain at Mladenovatz after her death.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: Serbia was devastated by epidemics and famine after the Austrians invaded and left behind many prisoners and disease. The Scottish Women’s Hospitals went there to treat the Serbian people, and Serbia later commemorated their work and Dr. Elsie Inglis.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: Dr. Elsie Inglis directed the equipment and overseas transport of the hospital units and received sustaining cooperation from the Admiralty and Foreign Office. She took personal charge of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals in Serbia in 1915 and was praised for her courage, judgment, endurance, and devotion. She died on 27 November 1917, and the Serbs commemorated her with a fountain at Mladenovatz.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals were staffed by women and served abroad with armies fighting a common foe. Their units treated patients suffering from typhus, typhoid, famine fevers, and other conditions in Serbia, and later served with the Serbian army in Russia. Their conduct upheld Britain’s honour and good faith amid the sufferings of the Russian people.

records.l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The First Serbian Unit was led by Dr. Eleanor Soltau. It worked in Serbia during the typhus epidemic and was among the Scottish women who went directly to crowded hospitals treating dying patients.

records.l: Dr. Eleanor Soltau, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: Dr. Eleanor Soltau was in charge of the First Serbian Unit until she became ill with diphtheria in the spring of 1915. She worked amid the typhus epidemic that was devastating the Serbian people.

records.l: Foreign Office, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The Foreign Office cooperated with Dr. Elsie Inglis and was responsible for the safety of the British outpost hospitals. It imposed stipulations that Dr. Inglis accepted when they did not hinder her work, and it undertook extensive care and diplomatic work on behalf of the hospitals.

records.l: Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: A Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit served with the Serbian army in Russia. The text says that, at the end of the unit’s service there, the Foreign Office was gravely concerned about its safety amid the chaotic sufferings of the Russian people.

records.l: Serbian nation, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The Serbian people suffered from epidemics, famine, and crowded hospitals after the Austrians invaded. The Scottish women went directly to their aid, and the Serbian nation later commemorated Dr. Elsie Inglis and their work.

records.l: the typhus epidemic, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The typhus epidemic was devastating the Serbian people in the spring of 1915. It formed the setting for the Scottish women’s work in crowded hospitals and contributed to the severe dangers and privations they endured.

records.l: Mladenovatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: At Mladenovatz, the Serbian nation built a beautiful fountain close to the camp hospital to commemorate Dr. Elsie Inglis and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. The fountain was formally opened on 7 October 1915 with a religious service according to the rites of the Greek Church.

records.l: simple fountain (in Mladenovatz), Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The fountain at Mladenovatz was built by the Serbs in grateful memory of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ work. Dr. Elsie Inglis turned on its water at its opening, and it was intended to flow through the coming years in remembrance of that work.

records.l: World War I, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The unit places the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ service in the period of the Allied armies, the Serbian army, and the fighting against a common foe. It records their work in Serbia and Russia during 1915 and commemorates Dr. Elsie Inglis’s death in 1917.

records.l: women’s courage and service in wartime, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER IX SERBIA ‘Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children.
records.s: The Scottish women faced epidemics, famine, danger, and severe privations without faltering in courage or endurance. Their service was presented as evidence of the power of womanhood to turn war’s curse toward blessing and to answer hatred with love.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The unit recounts Dr. Elsie Inglis’s accounts of the typhus epidemic, the German, Bulgarian, and Austrian invasion of Serbia, and the Serbian retreat of 1915. It describes the medical work of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals for Foreign Service and other British and American units, especially at Kragujevatz, and records the deaths and illnesses caused by typhus. It also relates the capture, imprisonment, and eventual liberation of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit, as well as Inglis’s determination and leadership. Letters from 1915 describe the unit’s hospitals, its work among Serbian patients, and conditions in Serbia.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: Elsie Inglis led the Scottish Women’s Hospitals work in Serbia, organised hospitals and medical responses, and refused to sign a German statement claiming that British prisoners had been well treated. She personally returned through deep snow to bring three members of her unit to the train and, after liberation, immediately began planning future work.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: Serbia suffered the Austrian invasion, a severe typhus epidemic, and the later invasion by German, Bulgarian, and Austrian forces. Its army and people endured retreat and enormous losses, while Serbian women maintained agriculture and Serbian medical workers and civilians supported the hospitals.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals for Foreign Service sent doctors, nurses, and supplies to Serbia and worked in hospitals, infectious-disease units, and disinfecting centres. Its members continued working during the typhus epidemic, suffering three deaths and nine cases of illness in one unit.

records.l: the Allied nations, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The Allies were expected by the Serbs to come to their aid, but they did not prevent the Bulgarian mobilisation or provide help during the invasion. Their failure to intervene left Serbia exposed to the attack from the north and east.

records.l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The Serbian army had defeated its enemy in 1914 and was regarded by the Serbs as the only army among the Great Powers’ forces to have done so. In 1915 it shortened its defensive line but could not withstand the German long-distance guns; 160,000 men escaped during the retreat.

records.l: Kragujevatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: Kragujevatz housed the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit in a girls’ school and included surgical, typhus, and general-disease hospitals. The first unit under Dr. Soltau also did excellent work there after the Serbian victories in 1914.

records.l: the First World War, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The First World War forms the setting for the invasion of Serbia, the typhus epidemic, the retreat, and the medical work described in the unit. The text also refers to the great cause for which Britain was standing in the war.

records.l: the typhus epidemic, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The typhus epidemic began in hospitals left filthy and overcrowded after the Austrian invasion and swept across Serbia. It raged for three months, killed 125 of Serbia’s 425 doctors, and affected two-thirds of the remainder.

records.l: the Serbian retreat of 1915, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The Serbian retreat of 1915 began after German forces appeared on the northern frontier, Bulgaria invaded from the east, and Austria advanced from the west. The Serbian army was caught in a trap, but 160,000 of its soldiers escaped.

records.l: the German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia formed part of the wider attack that began in autumn 1915, with 100,000 Germans massing in the north and Bulgarian forces invading from the east. The attack, joined by Austrian forces from the west, overwhelmed the Serbian defensive position.

records.l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit at Kragujevatz nursed 550 beds in three hospitals, including surgical, typhus, and general-disease wards. It equipped a surgical hospital with an X-ray room and operating theatre and later prepared to establish a disinfecting centre at Mladanovatz.

records.l: the typhus disease, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: Typhus disease spread through Serbia after the Austrian invasion and caused extensive deaths among Serbian doctors and medical staff. The Scottish Women’s Hospitals treated it in infectious-disease hospitals and established or planned disinfecting work to control it.

records.l: the work of women in wartime, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
records.s: The women working in the Scottish units continued through the typhus epidemic, with none asking to leave; three died and nine became ill in one unit. Serbian women also kept the country’s agriculture going through four wars in three years, and Serbia planned a special medal to honour them.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: This unit concerns Dr. Elsie Inglis and the Scottish women who continued nursing Serbian wounded during the Austro-German invasion and occupation of Serbia in 1915. The Scottish hospital units chose whether to evacuate or remain with their patients; the unit at Krushieevatz stayed and treated as many as 1,200 people under severe overcrowding, cold, hunger, and scarcity. The women also undertook sanitation, laundry, bathing, and infection-prevention work, avoiding a recurrence of typhus. In February 1916, the remaining unit was sent under guard through Austria to Zürich, after which Dr. Inglis returned to Britain determined to advocate for Serbia.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Serbia was overrun by Austro-German forces in 1915 after its army was outnumbered by Austrians, Germans, Magyars, and Bulgarians. Its population suffered invasion, retreat, hunger, cold, displacement, and the imprisonment of its soldiers, while Dr. Elsie Inglis returned determined to work for its welfare.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Dr. Elsie Inglis led or served with the Scottish medical effort in Serbia, insisting that the unit remain with its wounded patients when evacuation became difficult. After months of service under occupation and captivity, she returned to Britain physically changed but committed to public advocacy and further work for the Serbian people.

records.l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Scottish hospital unit reorganised itself as tent hospitals, worked near the front, and later remained with Serbian wounded during the Austro-German invasion. At Krushieevatz it treated extreme numbers of patients, managed sanitation and laundry, and endured occupation before being sent north under guard in February 1916.

records.l: Serbian wounded, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Serbian wounded filled the hospitals during the retreat and occupation. The Scottish women refused to abandon them, caring for them in overcrowded buildings, corridors, outhouses, and makeshift wards despite shortages of beds, food, warmth, and medical resources.

records.l: Austro-German forces, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Austro-German forces overran Serbia in 1915 and took control of areas containing Scottish medical units and Serbian hospitals. They later guarded the Scottish unit as it was sent north toward Austria.

records.l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Serbian army was unable to resist the combined Austrians, Germans, Magyars, and Bulgarians, who were about four times its numbers. Its retreat left hospitals full of wounded and produced streams of soldiers, stragglers, and refugees.

records.l: the Allied nations, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Allies are presented as having failed to prevent the German breakthrough toward the Turks or to provide timely relief for Serbia. The Scottish unit nevertheless hoped that Allied action, including British troops at Salonika, might eventually help.

records.l: Sir Ralph Paget, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Sir Ralph Paget considered the evacuation of the British unit and, after recognising that its equipment could not be saved, allowed members to choose whether to leave or remain with their wounded. He eventually agreed that the unit should stand by its hospitals.

records.l: Krushieevatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Krushieevatz became the location where the Scottish unit remained during the Austro-German occupation. Its military hospital held 900 wounded in November 1915 and later as many as 1,200 patients, while the town and surrounding country suffered cold, hunger, refugees, prisoners, and military collapse.

records.l: Salonika, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Salonika was the destination where some equipment was believed to be safe and where a distant force of 150,000 British troops was expected. The unit doubted that this prospect would quickly relieve the famine and cold in the remaining Serbian territory.

records.l: the typhus epidemic, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Typhus had been a major earlier calamity, but the Scottish unit feared its return amid overcrowding, underfeeding, fatigue, and depression. Through cleaning, sanitation, laundry, bathing, and education about the connection between dirt and typhus, the unit recorded no cases of the disease in its hospital.

records.l: the German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Austro-German invasion caused Serbia's military collapse, the flight of refugees, the capture of soldiers, and the abandonment or occupation of hospitals. It forced the Scottish units to decide between retreat and remaining with their wounded patients.

records.l: evacuation of the hospital units, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Evacuation was considered during the invasion, with one possible route through Montenegro. Two parties retreated with the Serbs, while the unit at Krushieevatz stayed after its members were offered the choice of leaving or remaining; later, the remaining unit was transported under guard.

records.l: captivity of the Scottish unit, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Scottish unit spent about five months serving under foreign occupation and caring for Serbian wounded. On February 11, 1916, its members were sent north under Austrian guard with fixed bayonets, traveling through Vienna and eventually reaching Zürich.

records.l: Serbian military hospital at Krushieevatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Serbian military hospital at Krushieevatz housed about 900 wounded when the Scottish unit arrived, with the number later rising to 1,200 despite accommodation designed for 400 beds. The unit also assumed responsibility for the hospital's sanitation and laundry and converted corridors, outhouses, a magazine, and other spaces into treatment areas.

records.l: the Zoo, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The Zoo was the Scottish Sisters' name for the hospital magazine, where wounded patients occupied three tiers of shelving and later overcrowded makeshift spaces. In dim light, patients received beans and moved among the shelves, creating a scene Dr. Inglis remembered as unforgettable.

records.l: famine in Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Famine threatened the parts of Serbia left outside enemy control, alongside cold and displacement. The unit observed starving civilians, weakened workers, underfed prisoners, and exhausted oxen, while its own limited supplies could not feed all the hungry people around the hospital.

records.l: sanitation, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: The unit undertook sanitation work despite having no specialist, burying rubbish, emptying an overflowing cesspool, building incinerators, and repeatedly cleaning the hospital compound. It also established laundry and bathing arrangements, helping prevent typhus under severely overcrowded conditions.

records.l: Serbian prisoners, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ As the fever died out, a worse enemy came in.
records.s: Serbian prisoners arrived daily, sometimes by the thousands, and were sent north while the sick remained at the hospital. They endured hunger, cold, forced marches, inadequate shelter, and the loss of firewood, while those placed in the wards often arrived unwashed and infested with lice.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Dr. Elsie Maud Inglis returned to England in 1916 and led efforts to organize a final Scottish Women’s Hospitals enterprise for the Serbian Army on the Rumanian Russian front. After the War Office refused her request to serve in Basra, she organized a hospital unit and transport section of eighty women, which traveled via Archangel and Russia toward Odessa and the Dobrudja. The unit served wounded Serbian forces during the retreat, while the Russian Revolution endangered the Serbian Army and disrupted communications. Inglis continued working despite severe illness and returned to England in 1917, leaving the Serbian Division as the subject of her last recorded praise.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Dr. Elsie Maud Inglis returned to England in 1916, helped organize Kossovo Day, and planned a final Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army. After being refused permission to serve in Basra, she secured authorization for the Serbian enterprise and traveled with the unit via Archangel through Russia to Odessa and the Dobrudja. She continued directing the unit despite exhaustion and illness, and returned to England in 1917 after arranging its affairs and interviewing its members.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals depended on home committees to manage finance, personnel, equipment, transport, government relations, and logistical obstacles. Its final enterprise was a hospital unit and transport section for the Serbian Army, staffed initially by eighty women.

records.l: the S.W.H. Committees, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The S.W.H. Committees carried the main burden of finance and administration while Dr. Inglis served abroad. They selected personnel, supervised equipment and motor transport, dealt with government departments, supported Kossovo Day, and received Inglis’s reports from the Serbian mission.

records.l: Kossovo Day, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Kossovo Day was organized in Great Britain under Dr. Inglis’s chairmanship within six weeks. Hundreds of lectures on Serbian history were arranged throughout the country, and the flag-day was reported as a success.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Serbia was the subject of Kossovo Day and of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ continuing service. Dr. Inglis had already worked in Serbia and sought through Russia to learn more about the Serbs of Austria and the Jugoslavs.

records.l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Serbian Army was served by the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit on the Rumanian Russian front. During the retreat, the unit treated wounded soldiers, and Dr. Inglis insisted that she would return with the Serbian Army rather than leave it.

records.l: Serbian Volunteers, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Serbian Volunteers were intended to be served by the final Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit on the Rumanian Russian front.

records.l: Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Russia was the route and field of service for Dr. Inglis and her unit, which traveled from Archangel through Moscow toward Odessa. The unit encountered Russian officials and civilians who provided trains, food, repairs, transport assistance, and other support.

records.l: Russian Revolution, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Russian Revolution imperilled the safety of the Serbian Army on the Rumanian front and cut communications with Dr. Inglis’s unit. Inglis sent members home with important verbal messages while the London Committee awaited news and urged her return.

records.l: Rumania, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Rumania was the location of the Serbian Army’s retreat and of major Scottish Women’s Hospitals work. At Galatz, Rumania, Dr. Inglis, her doctors, and nurses treated masses of wounded and performed operations and dressings for fifty-eight of sixty-three hours.

records.l: Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Odessa was the destination of the unit’s journey through Russia and the place from which Dr. Inglis sent her last letter in June 1917. Her final words from Odessa praised the Serbian Division as superb and expressed pride in being attached to it.

records.l: Archangel, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: Archangel was the unit’s entry point into Russia. British naval personnel and local officials helped organize the city, arrange a special train and berths, provide supplies, and send the unit onward with extensive hospitality and ceremony.

records.l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army consisted initially of eighty women and a transport section. It sailed with fourteen cars, traveled via Archangel and Moscow, and was prepared to treat wounded Serbian forces on the Rumanian Russian front.

records.l: the journey from Archangel to Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Russian journey took the unit from Archangel toward Moscow by special train after a rapid passage through Archangel. The travelers experienced delays, repaired couplings and engines, received food and other assistance from Russian authorities, and were welcomed by Russian soldiers and civilians.

records.l: the British Government, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The British Government refused Dr. Inglis permission to take a fully equipped unit to Basra, though the refusal was described as insulting. It later permitted her journey with the Serbian unit and assured the committees that the unit was safe and that its return would be expedited.

records.l: the Serbian retreat of 1915, Dr. Elsie Inglis, CHAPTER X RUSSIA 1917 ‘Even so in our mortal journey, The bitter north winds blow, And thus upon life’s red river, Our hearts as oarsmen row.
records.s: The Serbian retreat produced large numbers of wounded whom the Scottish Women’s Hospitals treated. At Galatz, the unit worked continuously for fifty-eight of sixty-three hours while performing operations and dressings.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Elsie describes the British medical unit’s journey from Archangel through Moscow and Odessa to the Serbian 1st Division, and its work during the fighting and retreat from Medgidia. The unit established hospitals at Medgidia and Bulbulmic, treated and evacuated wounded, and then helped care for thousands of neglected patients at Braila. Elsie reports strong Russian and Serbian support, the bravery of the Serbs, and severe shortages of medical staff and facilities. By January 1917, the unit was operating a hospital at Reni and trying to secure more Serbian patients and organize Serbian hospital work.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Elsie led and reported on the British medical unit during its journey through Russia, its deployment with the Serbian 1st Division, and its retreat from Medgidia. She organized hospital work, arranged evacuations, sought additional medical support, and helped care for wounded at Braila and Reni.

records.l: the unit (British medical unit), Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The unit traveled from Archangel through Moscow and Odessa to the Serbian 1st Division. It established and operated hospitals at Medgidia and Bulbulmic, evacuated equipment and personnel during the retreat, and later helped treat wounded at Braila and Reni; Elsie considered its members energetic, cheerful, and exceptionally brave.

records.l: the Serbian medical units, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The Serbian medical units included two small field hospitals assigned to serve a whole division. Elsie sought to establish a Serbian hospital and tried to coordinate with Serbian Hospital H. 2, while Serbian wounded were generally evacuated directly to Odessa.

records.l: Jugoslav Division, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The 1st Division was commanded by General Haditch and was described as being at an important point in the war, called a second Verdun. Its Serbian soldiers fought against General Mackensen and were praised by Russian officers as heroes for their actions in the fighting in the middle of September.

records.l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The Serbs received strong support and admiration in Russia, and Serbian officers and soldiers helped the unit during its journey and operations. Serbian wounded were evacuated to Odessa, while Russian officials and officers praised the Serbian soldiers for their courage and endurance.

records.l: Russians, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Russian officials along the railway and in Odessa assisted the unit generously. Russian hospitals took Serbian patients when possible, Russian soldiers helped the unit obtain water, and Russian officers praised the Serbian troops; Russian wounded also formed most of the patients received by the unit.

records.l: Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Odessa gave the unit an enthusiastic reception, with Russian officials, the consul, Serbian officers, transport, quarters, and public celebrations assisting or welcoming them. The city was deeply interested in the unit, and Elsie later returned there to investigate why Serbian patients were not being sent to the hospital.

records.l: Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Reni was a small village and an important junction with shipping and a crowded wharf. By January 1917 the unit had established a hospital there for badly wounded patients in connection with the evacuation station, though the unfinished building was difficult to heat.

records.l: Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Medgidia was the site of the unit’s main hospital, housed in a barrack, with personnel living in tents on the opposite hill. The unit arrived during the offensive, made the hospital operational within forty-eight hours, and remained there for less than three weeks before retreating.

records.l: Braila, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: Braila received an enormous influx of wounded during the retreat, with approximately 7,000 to 11,000 patients and only seven doctors, one of them a surgeon. The unit went there to help, found wounded lying in houses and without dressed wounds for several days, and worked until the immediate pressure had passed.

records.l: the retreat from Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The retreat began with the field hospital being moved back, followed by the transport and then the hospital personnel. Refugees and disorganized Russian, Serbian, and Rumanian soldiers crowded the roads, equipment and belongings were abandoned, and the unit moved through Caramacat and Hershova before reaching Braila.

records.l: World War I, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The war placed the Serbian 1st Division in a major battle against General Mackensen and produced intense pressure on medical services. It also caused repeated retreats, vast movements of refugees and soldiers, overcrowded hospitals, and severe demands on the British women serving with the unit.

records.l: the evacuation of Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The evacuation of Medgidia required the unit to dismantle and move its hospital equipment while continuing to nurse, operate, and evacuate patients. The transport and personnel were sent away in stages, and the unit ultimately lost two cars, one Ludgate boiler, and one box of radiators.

records.l: the hospital at Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The hospital at Medgidia was established in a barrack and made ready for patients within forty-eight hours of the unit’s arrival. The unit unpacked and repacked its equipment there, operated and nursed patients, and evacuated the hospital during the retreat.

records.l: the field hospital at Bulbulmic, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The field hospital at Bulbulmic was about seven miles from the front. It was brought back five versts at the beginning of the retreat, after which its transport and personnel were moved onward.

records.l: the shortage of medical staff, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘NEARING ODESSA, ‘_Sep.
records.s: The shortage of medical staff was severe at Braila, where 11,000 wounded were initially reported and only seven doctors were available, including one surgeon. Elsie also noted that the two small field hospitals had to serve an entire division and requested another base hospital to replace British Red Cross units moving with the 2nd Division.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Elsie writes from an ambulance train near Odessa and from the hospital at Reni about her medical unit's work among Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian patients during the war. She describes harsh weather, refugees, shortages, religious services, hospital inspections, and the unit's receipt of St. George Medals. She reports enthusiasm among Russian officers and patients for the changes in Petrograd and describes the unit's Easter observances. She also recounts a spy incident in which the unit was suspected but ultimately cleared and thanked for its conduct.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Elsie serves as a doctor and commandant with a medical unit working in hospitals and on an ambulance train in the war area. She describes managing hospital cleanliness, orderlies, patients, transport, religious services, and the unit's response to the spy incident.

records.l: Russians, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Russian soldiers and citizens express respect and gratitude toward Elsie and her unit. They welcome the changes in Petrograd, attend religious services, and emphasize their hope in the Allied cause and England.

records.l: Russian soldiers, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Russian patients are treated by Elsie's unit at Reni and are described as grateful, pleased by the unit's St. George Medals, and supportive during the spy incident. They received cigarettes and Easter eggs, and participated in religious services.

records.l: the unit (British medical unit), Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: The unit works in hospitals at Medgidia, Braila, Galatz, Reni, and elsewhere, caring for Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian patients. It faces severe cold, mud, fuel shortages, overcrowding, and suspicion of espionage, but is praised for its care and conduct.

records.l: England, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: England is regarded by people at the front as a strong power that can help put things right. Elsie says the unit remained at Reni during the spy incident partly to protect England's reputation among Russian soldiers.

records.l: Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Russia is experiencing political change and remains a major war area in which Elsie's unit operates. Russian people are described as religious, interested in England, and hopeful about the future after the war.

records.l: Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Odessa is named as the place near which Elsie writes on January 25, 1917, from an ambulance train.

records.l: Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Reni is the location of the unit's hospital and several of Elsie's letters. The hospital experiences severe snow, mud, fuel shortages, and a frozen Danube, while continuing to care for Russian Army and Navy patients.

records.l: Galatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: At Galatz, the unit operates a hospital in a school and later works in connection with Reni. Elsie recalls that the unit worked through the night there and that an armoured car section sent a messenger from Galatz to fetch General Kropensky during the spy incident.

records.l: Danube, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: The Danube freezes completely near Reni, reportedly for the first time in seven years. Cossack soldiers cross it to cut wood for the hospital.

records.l: Petrograd, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: News from Petrograd causes excitement among Elsie and her unit. Russian officers and patients generally support the change and describe it as a significant political development.

records.l: the ambulance train, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Elsie writes from an ambulance train near Odessa after the unit has worked in hospitals for Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian patients. The train's movement brings the unit close to the front, where it narrowly leaves before a station is burned.

records.l: Scottish Women's Hospital at Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: The hospital at Reni treats soldiers and sailors from different parts of Russia and is inspected for cleanliness, food, nursing, and medical care. It receives religious blessings, gives Easter gifts to patients, and continues operating despite mud, weather, fuel shortages, and the spy investigation.

records.l: the First World War, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: The war causes deserted villages, streams of refugees, destroyed stations, burning fuel tanks and grain ricks, disrupted schooling, and difficult conditions for hospitals. Elsie contrasts these effects with the relative safety of Scotland.

records.l: Russian Revolution, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: The Russian Revolution is associated with the changes reported from Petrograd. Elsie observes that Russian officers and patients support the change and that revolutionary conditions contribute to suspicion during the spy incident.

records.l: Easter, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: At Easter, Russian patients and soldiers thank Elsie and her unit for their care and express hope in the Allied cause. The unit attends or holds services, sings Easter hymns, exchanges Russian greetings, and gives patients Easter eggs and cigarettes.

records.l: refugees, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: Refugees in the Dobrudja travel in crowded carts carrying salvaged furniture, pots, pans, pigs, and children. Elsie describes villages along their route as deserted.

records.l: spy incident, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ ‘IN AN AMBULANCE TRAIN, ‘NEAR ODESSA, _Jan.
records.s: During the spy incident, the unit is suspected because it is a foreign hospital near the front while spy fever and revolutionary unrest are widespread. General Kropensky helps resolve the matter, the unit is cleared and apologized to, and Elsie says its conduct preserved Russian confidence in England.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: These letters record Elsie Maud Inglis’s work with the Scottish Women’s Hospitals at Reni in 1917, caring for Russian and Serbian personnel during World War I. She describes the hospital’s relations with Russian soldiers and officials, its shortages, patients, staff, and wartime activities. In August the Reni hospital closed and the unit rejoined the Serbian Division at the front, while Inglis praised the discipline and fighting qualities of the Serbs. By October the Division was preparing to move, and in November Inglis wrote from Archangel that she was on her way home.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Elsie Maud Inglis directs and describes the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ work at Reni, including its medical care, relations with Russian officials and soldiers, and movement with the Serbian Division. She reports on patients, shortages, operations, riding, and the hospital’s closure before rejoining the Division.

records.l: Mrs. Flinders Petrie, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Mrs. Flinders Petrie receives Inglis’s letters and is praised for encouraging subscriptions to the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. Inglis asks her to press for faster dispatch of relief personnel and sends regards to Professor Flinders Petrie.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals operate a hospital at Reni, raise funds, and supply personnel and equipment despite wartime delays. Their Reni work lasts eight months before the hospital closes and the unit rejoins the Serbian Division.

records.l: Jugoslav Division, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The Serbian Division is expected to take the hospital unit back into its service after the Reni work ends. Inglis rejoins the Division in August and is later with it at Hadji Abdul while preparations are made for another move.

records.l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Inglis says that Serbs, including the soldiers in the Division, are regarded as magnificent, disciplined fighting men whose presence could stiffen Russian troops. Serbian orderlies in the hospital are described as quick, devoted, and a great comfort.

records.l: Russians, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The Russians are described as a fascinating people, especially the common soldier. Russian soldiers support the hospital, while Russian patients receive treatment from the English Sisters.

records.l: Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Russia is presented as undergoing a major upheaval that has changed the tone and attitude of its soldiers. Inglis’s work takes place in Russian territory, amid uncertainty about military and political changes.

records.l: Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Reni is the site of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ hospital, which Inglis describes as being beside the Danube and surrounded by the Steppe. The hospital remains there until it closes in August 1917.

records.l: Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Inglis writes from Odessa in June and August 1917 while the Reni work is being wound up and arrangements are made to join the Serbian Division. She reports that the Reni hospital is full and busy before its closure.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Serbia is the home of the patient Nicolai, who describes his family, garden, and former intention to become a smith. Inglis also discusses the importance of the Serbian military presence and its connection with the Division.

records.l: the Eastern front, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The hospital is praised by Russian soldiers as the best hospital on this front. Inglis says the Serbian troops are wanted at the front to strengthen Russian forces.

records.l: Scottish Women's Hospital at Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospital at Reni treats Russian and Serbian patients, including wounded soldiers and a ten-year-old boy. Russian soldiers defend its reputation and insist that the Commandant provide whatever it needs.

records.l: Russian soldiers, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: Russian soldiers tell the local Commandant that the Scottish hospital is the best hospital on the front and must receive whatever it wants. They are also described as friendly toward the hospital and as displaying a changed political and social attitude.

records.l: Russian Revolution, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The unit refers to the great reverberation that has shaken Russia and to a new tone among Russian soldiers. It does not name the Russian Revolution directly, but connects the soldiers’ changed attitude with the upheaval in Russia.

records.l: hospital closure and transfer to the Serbian Division, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The Reni hospital closes in late August 1917 after eight months of work. Its personnel join the Serbian Division, while the hospital has been full of mostly Russian patients and busy with emergency operations.

records.l: World War I, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The letters describe wartime hospital work, military movements, bombardment and air raids, wounded soldiers, military shortages, and the effects of the conflict on Russia, Serbia, and other European nations.

records.l: Russian and Serbian military medical work, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ‘_On Active Service.
records.s: The unit provides medical care to Russian and Serbian soldiers, performs prolonged operations, manages shortages of equipment and relief personnel, and works alongside military formations. Its medical work continues at Reni before transferring with the Serbian Division.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: This unit recounts Dr. Elsie Inglis’s final work leading her unit during the Serbian evacuation from Russia and her return voyage to England. She insisted on preserving the equipment, supporting the Serbian Army, and bringing the Serbian soldiers safely away from the Russian front. Gravely ill, she organized the journey, continued working aboard the transport, and reached Newcastle, where she died surrounded by her relatives and members of the unit. Her final words present death as a passage into a new life and an encounter with God.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: Dr. Elsie Inglis directed her unit through bombardments, retreats, evacuations, and the Serbian evacuation from Russia, always insisting that the equipment be preserved. Though suffering from dysentery and extreme weakness, she organized the journey west, cared for Serbian soldiers and members of her unit, and continued planning future work until shortly before her death in Newcastle.

records.l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The unit worked night and day during the evacuations, overcoming disorder and transporting its equipment safely. Its members accompanied Dr. Inglis and Serbian soldiers on the journey west, cared for her during her final illness, and recorded her courage, discipline, kindness, and consideration.

records.l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The Serbian Army suffered severe losses in fighting after the Rumanians broke, with 11,000 men lost from a division of 15,000. Representatives of the Serbian Army travelled with Dr. Inglis and her unit, and she insisted that they be brought away from the Russian front.

records.l: Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: Russia was the setting of the retreats, bombardments, uncertainty, and evacuation described in this unit. Dr. Inglis worked there with her unit and sought to secure the Serbian Army's removal from the Russian front.

records.l: Galatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: Galatz was the place to which the hospitals were ordered to fall back. The unit's equipment was brought safely there after Miss Borrowman and Miss Brown followed trucks that had been carried away with a refugee train.

records.l: Newcastle, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: Newcastle was the port where the transport arrived after its dangerous voyage west. Dr. Inglis left the boat there on November 25, 1917, and died shortly afterward at the Station Hotel.

records.l: England, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: England represented to Dr. Inglis a quiet, strong, and invincible source of comfort behind the wartime confusion. She returned there with her unit and the Serbian representatives, though she died soon after reaching Newcastle.

records.l: the First World War, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The First World War forms the context for the bombardments, retreats, shortages, hospital evacuations, and dangers faced by Dr. Inglis, her unit, and the Serbian Army. The unit's return voyage also faced serious maritime dangers in wartime waters.

records.l: the Serbian evacuation from Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The Serbian evacuation from Russia was the central task that Dr. Inglis completed before her death. She sent wires, planned the movement, organized the journey, and travelled with the Serbian soldiers and her unit toward England.

records.l: Dr. Inglis's death, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: Dr. Inglis's death followed a prolonged illness, severe weakness, and a relapse during the voyage west. In Newcastle she spoke calmly of going to the other side, sent messages to those she remembered, heard words about the life beyond, and died peacefully.

records.l: the voyage west, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The voyage west carried Dr. Inglis, her unit, the H.G. Staff, and Serbian soldiers from Russia toward England. It included fifteen days on a train, a difficult embarkation at Archangel, a dangerous sea passage, and the near collision and breaking of the transport's moorings before arrival at Newcastle.

records.l: the captured transport ship, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The transport carried Dr. Inglis, her unit, and Serbian representatives toward England. During the voyage Dr. Inglis rested in a cabin, played patience, prescribed for an ill naval officer, and continued reviewing accounts and planning future work despite her illness.

records.l: the equipment, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The equipment was Dr. Inglis's constant concern during bombardments, retreats, and evacuations. Members of the unit recovered trucks carrying it after they went onto the wrong line, and ingenuity was used to bring it safely through to Galatz.

records.l: the moorings, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: The moorings of the transport broke during a storm after a large liner came within a foot of cutting the vessel in two. Dr. Inglis interpreted this event as an image of her own approaching death, saying that the same hand that had cut her moorings was cutting hers.

records.l: death and the afterlife, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ’ CHAPTER XI THE MOORINGS CUT ‘Not I, but my Unit.
records.s: Death and the afterlife are presented as a passage into fuller life rather than simple ending. Dr. Inglis spoke of starting a new job on the other side, and those present felt triumph, peace, and a glorious presence after she died.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Elsie Inglis returned to Edinburgh gravely ill after leading medical work for Serbia during the war and died on November 26, 1917. She was buried on November 29 in St. Giles’, with Allied flags, military honors, and representatives of Scotland, Serbia, her medical units, and her charitable work present. Crowds followed the procession across Edinburgh, and Serbian representatives carried her coffin to the grave. Her final message urged the London Committee for the Scottish Women’s Hospitals to support Serbian hospitals and transport.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Elsie Inglis returned to Edinburgh after serving abroad and died on November 26, 1917. She was buried with military honors and the flags of Great Britain and Serbia, and was remembered for her courage, service, and devotion to Serbia and Scotland.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals were represented at Elsie Inglis’s funeral by her colleagues, hospital and hostel officials, and the units she had led. In her last message, Inglis urged the London Committee to ensure that the Serbs received their hospitals and transport.

records.l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Edinburgh received Elsie Inglis’s body and held her funeral at St. Giles’. Large crowds, including many women and people connected with her charitable work, followed the procession across the city to her grave.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Serbia was represented at Elsie Inglis’s funeral by its Minister and members of its Legation. Inglis was remembered as an immortal link between Serbia and Scotland, and her final message asked that Serbian hospitals and transport be maintained.

records.l: Scotland, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Scotland honored Elsie Inglis with military recognition and a funeral attended by the chief of the Scottish Command. Scottish flags and banners appeared at her funeral, and the Dean described her as a link between Serbia and Scotland.

records.l: St. Giles’, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: St. Giles’ was the church where Elsie Inglis’s body was carried for the last time and where her funeral service took place. The Hallelujah Chorus was played as the procession left the church.

records.l: Serbian nation, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Representatives of the Serbian nation attended Elsie Inglis’s funeral as true-hearted mourners. They were granted the honor of carrying her coffin and lowering it into the grave.

records.l: Dr. Inglis's funeral and burial, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Elsie Inglis’s funeral took place on November 29, 1917, in the presence of her family, colleagues, representatives of societies, hospital officials, military personnel, and Serbian representatives. Her coffin, covered by Allied flags, was placed on a gun carriage, followed through Edinburgh by a large crowd, and carried to the grave by representatives of the Serbian nation.

records.l: the First World War, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: The funeral took place while war was ongoing, and Elsie Inglis was honored as a Red Cross worker who had served abroad. The service included military honors, Allied flags, and representatives of the nations connected with her wartime work.

records.l: Red Cross service, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: Elsie Inglis was honored as a worker and leader of the Red Cross whose service had aided Serbia and other people affected by the war. Her funeral included military honors for what was described as the service of a happy warrior of the Red Cross.

records.l: Dr. Inglis's last message, Dr. Elsie Inglis, ”’ As ‘We’ waited those anxious weeks for the news of the arrival of Dr.
records.s: In a message dated November 26, 1917, Elsie Inglis apologized for being unable to go to London and asked the Scottish Women’s Hospitals committee to meet Serbian representatives and show them hospitality. She specifically urged the committee to ensure that the Serbs had their hospitals and transport, thanked the committee for its kindness and support, and dictated the message to Miss Evelyn Simson.

records.l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: *Dr. Elsie Inglis*, by Lady Frances Balfour, is a memoir of the Scottish doctor, suffragist, institution-builder, and wartime medical leader Elsie Maud Inglis (1864–1917). Dedicated to Serbia and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, it draws on family, friends, patients, and hospital Units to portray a woman whose courage, religious faith, devotion to justice, and practical service shaped her life. The book begins with the Inglis family’s Scottish roots and far-reaching lives in America and India, then follows Elsie’s childhood in India. Her father, John Inglis, gave his daughters equal opportunities, encouraged intellectual companionship, and deeply influenced her sense of fairness and independence. After the family’s moves through Tasmania, Edinburgh, and Paris, her mother’s death placed household responsibilities on Elsie while she was still young. Elsie pursued medicine despite entrenched barriers against women students. She studied in Edinburgh and Glasgow, fought exclusions from clinical teaching, obtained the Triple Qualification, worked at the New Hospital for Women in London, and trained in midwifery at the Rotunda in Dublin. Her father’s death in 1894 was a profound loss. She later graduated M.B., C.M. in 1899, developed surgical skill, and worked to expand women’s medical education. Alongside medicine, Inglis championed women’s suffrage, Liberal politics, Home Rule, and women’s citizenship. She helped organize the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, opposed militancy, and became known as a fair, disciplined leader. In Edinburgh she helped establish Muir Hall of Residence and founded the Hospice in the High Street, serving mothers, infants, students, and poor families with both medical skill and personal care. Her faith, family, friendships, and disciplined habits sustained her. World War I redirected her work on an international scale. After the War Office rejected her offer of service, she organized the Scottish Women’s Hospitals through suffrage networks; French and Serbian authorities accepted them. The hospitals served in France, Serbia, and Russia. In Serbia, Inglis and her colleagues confronted typhus, famine, invasion, overcrowding, and shortages. Some Units remained with patients during the 1915 occupation, were captured, and later sent through Austria to Zürich. Returning to Britain, Inglis organized a final Unit for the Serbian Army on the Rumanian Russian front. Despite illness, revolution, retreats, disrupted communications, and severe shortages, she led work at Medgidia, Bulbulmic, Braila, and Reni, caring for Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian patients. Gravely ill, she helped evacuate the Serbian Army and her Unit from Russia, reached Newcastle, and died on November 26, 1917. Her funeral in Edinburgh united Scottish, Serbian, Allied, medical, and charitable representatives, while her final message urged continued support for Serbian hospitals and transport.

records.l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: This is a biographical record of Elsie Maud Inglis, a woman doctor, suffrage organiser, founder and leader of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, and wartime medical commander. Born at Naini Tal in August 1864, she grew up between India, Tasmania, Edinburgh, and Paris, close to her father John Inglis. From childhood she was intelligent, independent, observant, strong-willed, and inclined toward service. After her mother’s death she supported her father and recorded resolutions to be truthful, thorough, and responsible. She chose medicine, trained in Edinburgh and Glasgow, passed the Triple Qualification in 1892, worked at the New Hospital for Women in London and the Rotunda in Dublin, and later graduated M.B., C.M. from the University of Edinburgh. Her career combined practice, teaching, clinical study, and institution-building. In Edinburgh she practised with Dr. Jessie MacGregor, cared for poor and paying patients alike, lectured on gynecology, supported women’s medical education, founded Muir Hall for women students, and helped establish maternity and infant-welfare work. Her faith, family ties, self-command, and concern for justice informed her work. In politics she supported Liberalism, Home Rule, women’s suffrage, and women’s citizenship. As Honorary Secretary of the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, she organised workers and funds, opposed militant suffragism on legal and constitutional grounds, and sacrificed professional prospects for the franchise cause. She was also an early advocate of women sanitary inspectors. At the outbreak of the First World War, after the War Office rejected women’s medical service, she founded the Scottish Women’s Hospitals with support from suffrage societies. She raised funds, organised units, and led service abroad, particularly in Serbia and later with the Serbian Army in Russia. She endured occupation, captivity, bombardment, retreats, evacuations, shortages, illness, and exhausting medical work, refusing to abandon the Serbian Army and insisting on care for patients and preservation of equipment. She died while returning to Britain in November 1917 after service connected with the Serbian evacuation from Russia. She was buried with military honors and remembered for courage, justice, kindness, pioneering leadership, and devotion to Serbia, Scotland, women’s opportunities, and medical service.

records.l: Lady Frances Balfour, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Lady Frances Balfour authored Dr. Elsie Inglis, The Life of Lady Victoria Campbell, and Life and Letters of Rev. James Macgregor, D.D., and received a letter from Miss Burke concerning Dr. Elsie and hospitals.

records.l: London, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: London is a city central to Elsie Inglis’s hospital work, activities, and wartime proposals. From 1892 to 1893, she worked at the New Hospital for Women, assisted Garrett Anderson in an operation, and visited churches, sermons, theatres, and dances. In September 1914, she presented proposals there to the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies and the War Office; the London society later helped fund hospital units.

records.l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Serbia is a country and a major field of service for the Scottish Women’s Hospitals during the First World War. It has the Serbian army as its national army and is described as a lovely country with a beautiful landscape, but its central record is of devastation: Austrian invasion, a severe typhus epidemic, famine, and the 1915 German, Bulgarian, Austrian, and Austro-German invasion. Epidemics and disease followed the Austrians’ invasion, while enemy occupation brought hunger, cold, displacement, losses, and the imprisonment of soldiers. Outnumbered by Austrians, Germans, Magyars, and Bulgarians, Serbia’s army and people endured the Serbian retreat of 1915. Amid this suffering, Serbia received medical and nursing aid from the Scottish Women’s Hospitals for Foreign Service and assistance from Foreign Missions. The Scottish Women’s Hospitals treated Serbian people, sought to work with the Serbian army, and made Serbia one of their principal countries of service. Dr. Elsie Inglis became a committed supporter of the Serbian cause, worked there despite difficult travel and broken transport, returned determined to aid its welfare, and sought to maintain Serbian hospitals and transport. Serbian medical workers and civilians supported the hospitals, while Serbian women maintained agriculture during wartime; plans were made for a Serbian women’s medal to honor them after the war. Serbia later recognized and commemorated the women’s medical work and Dr. Elsie Inglis. It was associated with service and love from 1914 to 1917, represented at Inglis’s funeral by its Minister and Legation, and remembered through an enduring link between Serbia and Scotland. It also remained connected to Kossovo Day, the Serbian military presence, and Inglis’s interest in the Serbs of Austria and the Jugoslavs.

records.l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Scottish Women’s Hospitals was a women-run wartime medical organisation for foreign service, created through Scottish suffrage organisation and run as a Scottish Federation scheme. Formed after the War Office rejected Elsie Maud Inglis’s offer of service, it organised skilled women, raised funds, and planned efficient medical units, motor ambulances, and rest stations wherever needed. The National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies supported it through appeals, press notices, and fundraising, although public speakers were sometimes asked not to mention the suffrage cause that had supplied its organisation and workers. Its units, equipped and staffed entirely by women, sent doctors, nurses, supplies, personnel, and equipment overseas during the First World War. They worked in France, Belgium, Serbia, Corsica, and Russia, including at Royaumont, and provided help to Jugoslavs. In Serbia they served in hospitals, infectious-disease units, and disinfecting centres amid typhus, typhoid, famine fevers, and other suffering. Members continued work during the typhus epidemic despite illness and deaths in one unit. The organisation was identified by the Union Jack displayed with the red, white and green flag. Dr. Elsie Inglis organised the Hospitals and personally led work in Serbia in 1915. The organisation gave her intense surgical experience, including long periods at the operating table, and employed her abroad during wartime. Its work depended on home committees handling finance, personnel, equipment, transport, government relations, and other logistical obstacles. Its final enterprise was a hospital unit and transport section for the Serbian Army, initially staffed by eighty women. It operated a hospital at Reni for eight months before that hospital closed and the unit rejoined the Serbian Division. The Hospitals then served with the Serbian army in Russia. Inglis’s final message urged the London Committee to ensure that the Serbs received their hospitals and transport. Dedicated to Serbia and described as having served and loved its brethren from 1914 to 1917, the Scottish Women’s Hospitals became one of Inglis’s living memorials and were represented at her funeral by colleagues, officials, and units she had led.

records.l: the memoir of Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: A memoir of Elsie Inglis, compiled from family, friends, patients, Units, letters, and stories, seeks a transparently honest, affectionate, faithful portrait, tracing her life from its opening footsteps through the sands of time.

records.l: Elsie Inglis’s family and kindred, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: The records concern Elsie Inglis’s family and kindred, the Inglis family of Kingsmills in Inverness-shire. Descended from George Inglis’s Inverness branch, the family included generations who travelled or served abroad, notably in Carolina and India; its letters show energy, exploration, religious faith, and theological reflection. After Mr. Inglis retired, the family left India, with Sona, a household member and nurse, and spent two years in Hobart, Tasmania, settling two sons on land. They then made Edinburgh home at 70 Bruntsfield Place, where Elsie and Eva attended school and Elsie’s education in Paris was supported.

records.l: patients and local families, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Patients and local families regarded Dr. Inglis as a trusted and generous friend as well as a physician. She provided medical treatment, household advice, nursing, financial help, advocacy, and personal visits, often refusing payment and continuing to remember families and their circumstances after travelling abroad.

records.l: Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: The Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh opened in 1904 as an eight-bed maternity home with an operating theatre in a poorer district. It grew into a centre for maternity, infant-welfare, nursing, and medical education for women, training nurses for the Central Midwives Board examination and offering opportunities unavailable elsewhere. Its later facilities included a baby clinic, milk depot, health centres, and a malnutrition ward. Through its patients, it is associated with Elsie Inglis’s living memorials.

records.l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals units, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: The hospital units are intended as carefully selected, well-equipped teams staffed by women doctors, nurses, and ambulance workers. They are sent to Allied nations wherever wanted, and, as work expands, add motor ambulances and rest stations.

records.l: Scotland, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Scotland was the setting for much of Dr. Elsie Inglis’s suffrage organising, including her work in the Highlands and with the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies. Scottish women’s organised support later helped Inglis establish units and equipment for wartime medical work. Scotland honored Elsie Inglis with military recognition and a funeral attended by the chief of the Scottish Command. Scottish flags and banners appeared at her funeral, and the Dean described her as a link between Serbia and Scotland.

records.l: God, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Elsie was raised in a devout household and understood humanity as created in God’s image. She did not accept views that caused people to despise or underrate human work, and she sought to convince herself that a reasonable service was asked for and accepted by God.

records.l: Kingsmills, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Kingsmills, Inverness-shire, was held in 1740 by Hugh Inglis. His son George inherited it, and the Inglis family then living in Inverness descended from George.

records.l: Alexander Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Alexander Inglis was a merchant and property owner in Charleston. Around 1780 he emigrated to Carolina after marrying Mary Deas, leaving their four children to be educated in Scotland. He owned slaves and a pew in St. Michael’s Church, and supported the British Government and British constitution during the American conflict. His life ended in Charleston in 1791, when he was killed from wounds received in a duel.

records.l: David Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: David Inglis, Alexander’s son and Elsie Inglis’s grandfather, was raised in Scotland by his uncle William Inglis. He joined the East India Company as a writer in India in 1798, served in the Mahratta War in 1803, and administered the Peshwa’s territorial cessions under the Treaty of Bassein. He married Martha Money in 1806, later entered business in Bombay, and returned to England in 1812, living in Walthamstow. The records also identify him as a son of John Inglis and as a husband in John Inglis’s marriage counsel.

records.l: the British Government, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: The British Government refused Dr. Inglis permission to take a fully equipped unit to Basra, a refusal described as insulting. It later permitted her journey with the Serbian unit, protected the Serbian Army with the Scottish women serving it, assured committees of safety, and expedited the unit’s return.

records.l: Alexander Inglis’s duel, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Alexander Inglis’s duel followed what he described as a gross insult to his honour. Before the duel he wrote a letter to his children, explaining that he sought reparation as their natural guardian and protector; he was fatally wounded and died in 1791.

records.l: East India Company, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: The East India Company employed David Inglis and later his son John Inglis. It recognized David’s service in receiving the territorial cessions of the Peshwa and granted John Inglis a nomination to Haileybury College.

records.l: India, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: India is a place that shaped the careers and family life of David Inglis, John Inglis, Mr. Inglis, and Elsie Maud Inglis. It was the setting for official, military, and administrative work, including Mr. Inglis’s long public service as Chief Commissioner of Oude, as well as family separations and relationships with Indian servants and communities. Elsie’s early childhood was divided between the hot plains and the hills; the family travelled by palki and visited Naini Tal, giving her familiarity with long journeys and varied surroundings. The account concludes with the family leaving India after Mr. Inglis’s retirement and his later recollection of Elsie’s childhood walk, when she was believed lost.

records.l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: John Inglis was an Indian civil servant of the East India Company service, born in 1820. Taught by Rev. Dr. Niblock and educated at Haileybury from 1839, he entered Indian civil administration after learning the language in Calcutta. His career included service at Agra and in Punjab from 1847, participation in the suppression of the Indian Mutiny, appointment as Commissioner of Rohilcund from 1858 to 1868, service on the Board of Revenue and Legislative Council of India, and office as Chief Commissioner of Oude from 1875 to 1877. Lord Lytton praised his character and abilities, though Inglis did not sympathize with Lytton’s Afghan policy. He retired after long and arduous service. In 1846 he married Harriet Louis Thompson. They had daughters, including Elsie Inglis, and he was a devoted husband and affectionate, deeply involved father. He shared walks, breakfasts, letters, reading, and religious life with his daughters; sent Punch and Spectator weekly; and especially enjoyed an intellectual and affectionate fellowship with Elsie. He sought the best education and equal opportunities for all three sisters, supported women’s intellectual freedom and equality in family and public life, and regarded wives as husbands’ equal companions and confidential friends. His outlook encouraged Elsie’s independence, and he calmly and practically helped her overcome obstacles when she chose medicine, supporting her professional beginnings. His faith was broad, simple, profound, and central to his life; he believed the afterlife meant continued growth and learning. After retirement, the family moved to Tasmania and then Edinburgh, where they lived at 70 Bruntsfield Place and later in Melville Street. Following Mrs. Inglis’s death, he relied increasingly on Elsie, who shared his home, walked with him, and carried his burdens. A great walker, chivalrous and high-minded, he was remembered as upright, straightforward, and highly principled. He became seriously ill while Elsie was in Dublin, welcomed her return, and died patiently on 13 March 1894. His death left Elsie unable to imagine life without him, though she continued her work and supported his extended household.

records.l: Punjab, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: The Punjab was the province to which John Inglis was transferred in 1847 and where he served at Sealkote. He later returned during the Indian Mutiny and worked in the region during its settlement, gaining the confidence and affection of Sikhs, Punjabis, and Rajpoots.

records.l: John Lawrence, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: employs John Inglis [during and after suppression of the Mutiny] John Inglis worked beside John Lawrence during the suppression of the Indian Mutiny and afterward as part of the administration that settled the Punjab. John Inglis’s admiration for the northern peoples of India is presented in connection with this work.

records.l: Mrs. Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Mrs. Inglis, Harriet Louis Thompson, was John Inglis’s wife, daughter of an early Indian civilian, and one of nine sisters, most of whom married into the Indian Civil Service. An accomplished rider and driver and deeply religious, she lived in Southampton during a separation from her husband, where she founded and ran a large working-men’s club and gave Sunday religious lectures. As mother of Elsie Maud Inglis and her sisters, she carefully recorded their early development, taught them prayers and Bible lessons, and guided daily life. Remembered as quiet and strong, with an enduringly influential smile and eyes, she moved with her family from India to Tasmania and Edinburgh, corresponded with Elsie in Paris, and helped decide, through prayer with Mr. Inglis, that Elsie should go there. Soon after Elsie returned, Mrs. Inglis died of a virulent attack of scarlet fever.

records.l: Sona, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: Sona was an Indian ayah and long-serving household nurse to the Inglis family for more than thirty years. During the 1857 crisis, she accompanied some family members to England. She later became a Christian and was baptized in 1877. By the end of the account, she was regarded as one of the pillars of the Indian Christian Church in Lucknow.

records.l: Indian Mutiny, Dr. Elsie Inglis
records.s: affects John Inglis [prompted his return to India in 1858] The outbreak of the Indian Mutiny in 1857 caused John Inglis to return to India while Harriet Louis Thompson remained in England with six children and their ayah. John Inglis served in the suppression of the Mutiny, including the action at Najibabad, the recapture of Bareilly, and the pacification of Rohilcund.

records.l: British Empire in India, Dr. Elsie Inglis
